bio.en: Kevin Yien leads merchant product experiences at Stripe, previously built Square's restaurant business, and was Head of Product and Design at Mutiny.
bio.zh: 凯文·叶（Kevin Yien）在 Stripe 负责商户产品体验，此前在 Square 打造了餐饮业务，并曾任 Mutiny 的产品与设计负责人。

summary.en: Kevin argues every PM should be able to sell and support their own product, because if you can't, you can't be trusted to build it. He advocates keeping a decision log to build product sense through repeated reps and outcome review. The episode also covers his unconventional "unsell email" hiring tactic and practical uses of AI in PM work.
summary.zh: 凯文认为，每个 PM 都应该能卖、也能支持自己的产品，因为如果做不到，就不该被信任去构建它。他主张用"决策日志"通过反复决策与复盘结果来培养产品感。本期还涵盖了他非传统的"劝退邮件"招聘法，以及 AI 在 PM 工作中的实际应用。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: The PM job can become a little too internal, influencing my stakeholders and getting alignment and all these things. But if you can't sell or support your own product, I don't trust you to build the product.
turns.zh: 产品经理这个职位有时会变得过于关注内部事务，影响到利益相关方、协调各方意见等等。但如果你连自家产品都推销不出去、无法提供支持，我是绝不会信任你来负责产品开发的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You think every PM should keep a decision log?
turns.zh: 你觉得每个产品经理都应该保留决策日志吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: We all talk about product sense. To me, it's just a fancy way of saying you can make good decisions with insufficient data. PMs need as many reps as possible in making decisions, documenting the rationale behind those decisions, and then crucially seeing the outcome of them.
turns.zh: 我们总说产品洞察力。对我而言，这不过是用数据不足的情况下做决策的华丽说辞。产品经理需要尽可能多地积累决策经验，记录决策背后的逻辑，更关键的是要观察决策结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We have a lot of interesting approaches to hiring, including this idea of a unsell email.
turns.zh: 我们在招聘方面有很多有趣的做法，比如这封“不卖座邮件”。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: When you get to offer stage, I send an email and I say all the terrible things that are probably going to reinforce their fears. If you can tell them that upfront and they can read that whole email and still be equally excited to join you, find yourself a A+ hire.
turns.zh: 到了面试阶段，我会发邮件，把那些可能加剧候选人恐惧感的负面因素都罗列出来。如果你能提前坦诚告知，候选人读完邮件后依然热情满满地加入团队，那你就成功招到A+级人才了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious if you found any interesting uses of AI in your work.
turns.zh: 我很好奇你工作中有没有运用AI的有趣案例。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: We are not even beneath the dust on the surface when it comes to what's going to change.
turns.zh: 就产品变革而言，我们甚至还没触及皮毛。

(00:01:40): This episode is for anyone looking to become a better leader, thinker, and builder of products. The purpose of product management, not the person, but the practice, is to convert that potential into as much realized value for someone as possible, right? Minimum loss. When you're just getting started with a new product, the people that should be doing that are the people who are building it. That's an engineer, that's a designer, that's a sales person or a support person. They're the front line of the smallest loop possible to get something going, and it's through those practices that I think you're able to get the most exposure to what it takes to build a good product. (00:04:50): And then from there, that's your foundation. (00:07:54): Every PM has their definition of what is product management, and I have one that I'm trying to find exactly what I wrote, but essentially, it's to marshal the resources of your team to solve customer problems and drive business impact most efficiently, something like that. And I feel like it's very aligned with your perspective, but I really love this view of it's unlocking the potential energy of the team. Not just marshaling the resources of a team, but it's there, and your job is to maximize their effort. And this is why when people say, "I hate product managers. I don't want any product managers at my team. We don't need product managers here," I feel like that's often because you've had a bad PM. Good PMs make you better and make your life better, allow you to do the work you want to do and they take all the stuff you don't want to do, make sure the stuff you're doing is worthwhile. (00:08:38): Is there anything more you want to add along those lines?
turns.zh: 我知道导入错误数据可能会给客户带来诸多困扰，并迅速失去他们的信任。克里斯蒂娜，感谢你加入我们的讨论。如果你想了解更多信息，请访问oneschema.co。（00:07:54）：每位产品经理对产品管理都有自己的定义，我也曾试图准确找到我写下的定义，但本质上，产品管理就是要整合团队资源，最高效地解决客户问题并推动业务影响。（00:08:38）：你觉得这和你的观点很契合吗？是的，我非常认同你提到的释放团队潜能的观点。产品经理不只是整合团队资源，而是要激发团队的潜力，让他们的努力发挥最大价值。这也是为什么当人们说“我讨厌产品经理。我不想让团队有产品经理。我们不需要产品经理”时，往往是因为他们遇到了糟糕的产品经理。优秀的产品经理能提升团队效率，让你专注于核心工作，处理那些你不愿做的事务，确保你的工作有价值。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: To elaborate on that, I think the broader point is that truly not every team needs a product manager, but the activities, the outcome that one would drive needs to get done no matter what. And in some cases, this is why the prototypical companies that everyone references when they say, "They never had product managers, look at how successful they are," they're all building for themselves. Stripe, Twilio, Figma, designers for designers, engineers for engineers. When you are the customer, why the heck do you need someone else to help do the things that let you make decisions on what to build? But if you are not the customer, if you're working in a particularly complex space, if there's something that you, as the person that could build the product, feel you don't have, that's when you can essentially delegate that responsibility to someone else to say, "Hey, let me do the things I'm really good at and you do something that I need to get my job done." (00:09:39): So it's that sort of relationship that I think is often missing in the discourse. I think it would alleviate a lot of the, "We don't want PMs. PM is useless" or, "PM's one of the best thing since [inaudible 00:09:52]," which they're not. It's just a manifestation of that problem.
turns.zh: 进一步说，我认为更广泛的观点是，并非每个团队都需要产品经理，但无论如何，产品经理所推动的活动和成果都必须完成。在某些情况下，这就是为什么那些被视为典范的公司——比如Stripe、Twilio、Figma——都是为自己而建。设计师为设计师服务，工程师为工程师服务。当你是客户时，为什么还需要别人来帮你做决定呢？但如果你不是客户，如果你身处特别复杂的领域，如果你作为产品开发者觉得自己缺乏某些能力时，那你就可以把这些责任委托给别人，说：“嘿，让我专注于我擅长的事，而你负责我完成工作所需的部分。”（00:09:39）：这种合作关系正是我认为在讨论中常被忽视的。我认为这能缓解很多争议，比如“我们不需要产品经理。产品经理没用”或者“产品经理是自[00:09:52]以来最棒的东西之一”——事实并非如此。这只不过是问题的表象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Just to build on that, we're going on a tangent, but I think that's really interesting. I think there's another element of that, SNAP actually is another example where they waited, I think, until they had 200 people before they hired their first PM. To me, that's an example of other people were doing the PM job. As you said, there's PM activity, someone's doing them, lining people, prioritizing, making sure things are clear, making sure people aren't surprised, all these things PMs do. Someone's doing that, and my feeling is like, "Okay, your designers may love doing that, great. Let them do it." If your engineers that have a lot of product sense may want to do that, great. (00:10:28): But there's some point they either is like, "Forget it. I just want to code. I want to build that. I want to be sitting around in meetings all day," or they just aren't as good as things are scaling. And so it's kind of like, if your engineers, designers want to do it and are good at it, great. You don't need PMs for a long time. Oftentimes they're not good at it or they don't want to be sitting in doing all these PM things.
turns.zh: 是的。接下来，我们来延伸一下这个话题，虽然有点跑题，但我觉得这真的很有意思。我认为还有一个方面——Snap实际上也是一个例子，他们等到了有200名员工才聘请了首位产品经理。在我看来，这说明其他人也在承担产品经理的职责。正如你所说，产品经理的工作包括协调资源、设定优先级、确保沟通清晰、避免让团队惊讶等等。有人在做这些事，但我的感觉是，"好吧，也许设计师喜欢做这些事，太棒了。让他们去做吧。"如果工程师对产品有敏锐洞察力也想参与其中，那当然很好。但到了某个阶段，他们要么觉得，"算了，还是专心写代码吧。"要么就是随着团队规模扩大而力不从心。所以，如果你的工程师或设计师愿意承担这些职责并且做得不错，那没问题。短期内确实不需要专门的产品经理。但通常他们要么不擅长这些，要么不愿意参与这些繁琐的工作。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Yep, precisely.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so going back to the question of... So your advice is don't go straight into product management if you want to become a great PM. Where do you think people should start if they can? What are some options you recommend?
turns.zh: 好的，回到你的问题——如果你想成为一名出色的产品经理，最好别直接进入产品管理领域。如果可能的话，你建议人们从哪里起步？有哪些推荐的路径？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: The best way to think about this, in my opinion, is who were the people that you would be taking the PM responsibilities from and then do those jobs? And so for me, the sort of foundational three are going to be engineer, designer or salesperson. I think sales also gets not a bad rep, but a misrepresented reputation in tech where all they care about is quota, it's just about numbers, et cetera. In reality, the best salespeople are the best listeners, the best people at understanding the problem that the customer is having and then translating that into what you can do for them. And so if you get really good at having those calls, getting told no a lot, and being able to translate that, I mean, why would you not want to start there and then eventually move into something like product? So that's the foundational three for me.
turns.zh: 在我看来，最根本的三个起点是工程师、设计师或销售人员。说到销售，可能很多人对他们的印象不准确，认为他们只关心业绩指标、数字之类的。但实际上，最优秀的销售人员是倾听的高手，能理解客户的问题并转化为行动。所以如果你能精通这些沟通技巧、习惯被拒绝并能转化反馈，那为什么不从销售做起，再逐步转型到产品领域呢？这就是我认为的三个基础起点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So your advice is essentially if you want to be a PM, start as a designer or an engineer or a salesperson. I was an engineer, so this is exactly the path I went on. And I think there's an element of you start there and then you realize you're never going to be as amazing as the other people at that role and you're like, "Okay, maybe I should explore this other thing," because I was like, "I'm never going to be an amazing engineer. I'm good enough."
turns.zh: 所以你的建议基本上是，如果想成为产品经理，先从设计师、工程师或销售做起。我自己就是工程师出身，所以这正是我走过的路径。我发现一个现象，当你起步时，会意识到自己永远无法达到其他人的卓越水准，然后就会想，"或许我该探索其他领域"，因为我觉得，"我永远成不了顶尖工程师。我已经足够好了。"

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm like, "I'm pretty good at this other stuff. Let's explore that."
turns.zh: 我会想，"我对其他领域挺擅长的，那就探索一下吧。"

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: The one thing that I might tack on there, because this could lead to a negative perception, is, "Well, I'm never going to be a world-class engineer, world-class designer or et cetera, and so let me settle for being a PM." That could be the conclusion you arrive at, but I think a better way of framing it is, "I'm okay at those things. I'm potentially world-class at this other thing. Let me see what it feels like to double down on this area."
turns.zh: 唯一我想补充的是，因为这可能导致负面解读："好吧，我永远成不了世界级工程师、设计师之类的，那我就安心做产品经理吧。"这可能是人们得出的结论，但我认为更好的看法应该是，"我对那些领域还算擅长，但在其他领域或许能达到世界级水平。让我看看专注于这个领域的感觉如何。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对的。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: And I think that's just a good framing.
turns.zh: 我觉得这就是一个很好的框架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so let's talk about another insight and piece of advice that you have, is that you think that great PMs need to be great writers. I think a lot of people don't necessarily think this. I think people may probably think, "If I'm an okay writer, I can probably be really successful PM." Talk about why you think it's so important to be a really great writer to be a really great PM.
turns.zh: 好的，那让我们来谈谈你提到的另一个见解和建议——你认为优秀的产品经理必须是出色的写作者。我觉得很多人不一定这么认为。他们可能觉得：“如果我写作能力还行，就能成为非常成功的产品经理了。” 能否谈谈为什么你认为成为出色的产品经理，写作能力至关重要？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: It's actually shocking for me to hear that this isn't commonplace sort of acceptance, but the place that this comes from for me is, writing is clarity at scale, and a key component to a PM's job is creating clarity both internally and externally, but it is both sides of that that I think often get lost. A lot of times the PM job can become a little too internal, and it's about influencing my stakeholders and getting alignment and all these things. Don't get me wrong, all that's very important. You should write your PRDs, they should be super crisp, they should articulate things really well, but I'm not saying that every PM needs to be a marketer or a world-class copywriter, but you should be able to write really compelling messaging in the voice of the person that you're trying to serve. And I'm working backwards from the beliefs that, if you can't sell or support your own product, I don't trust you to build the product. And so that's where I think writing is the foundational component there.
turns.zh: 听到这不是普遍接受的观点，我还挺惊讶的。但对我来说，这源于一个观点：写作就是大规模的清晰表达，而产品经理工作的核心就是在内部和外部创造清晰性。然而这两个方面往往被忽视了。很多时候，产品经理的工作会变得过于关注内部，比如影响利益相关者、达成共识等等。我不是说这些不重要，你应该写好PRD（产品需求文档），它们必须非常清晰，信息传达要准确。但我不是说每个产品经理都得成为营销人员或世界级文案作者，而是你应该能够用服务对象的语气写出极具说服力的信息。我是从一个信念出发的：如果你连自己的产品都卖不出去、支持不了，那我就不相信你能做好产品。所以我认为写作是基础能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a few quotes I say often on this podcast just because they always come to mind. One is by Joan Didion who said that, "I don't know what I think until I've written it down." And that's what I find with writing where I need to actually write it down for me to really understand what the heck I'm thinking to really crystallize it.
turns.zh: 在播客里，我常引用琼·迪迪翁的一句话：“直到写下来，我才知道自己在想什么。” 我发现写作就是这样，我需要把想法写下来，才能真正理解自己在想什么，才能让它变得清晰。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Yeah, and I think writing is, it's both a mechanism for translating what you're trying to think into that thought into what you're actually trying to do, but then it needs additional revs to be properly consumed by everyone else. And that's I think the really hard part that a lot of folks don't do the extra mile effort to take on.
turns.zh: 是啊，我认为写作既是把你想的东西转化为行动的机制，但随后还需要多次润色，才能让其他人真正理解。这才是我认为很多人没有下功夫的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this to your earlier point of a job of PM is to unlock this potential energy of your team, of the various resources you have and obviously having everyone aligned behind a very, like, "This is what we are doing and everyone understanding it" and it being very clear is really powerful there. (00:15:06): Okay. So this begs the question, how does one become a great writer? What helped you become a better writer? How do you feel about your ability to write at this point?
turns.zh: 回到你之前提到的观点——产品经理的工作是释放团队的潜能，整合各种资源，让每个人都朝着一个目标齐心协力，“我们要做这件事，每个人都明白”，这种清晰的沟通非常重要。（00:15:06）：好的。那这就引出了一个问题：如何成为一个优秀的写作者？是什么帮助你提升了写作能力？你现在对自己的写作能力有何看法？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Oh man.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any advise on becoming better?
turns.zh: 有没有提升写作能力的建议？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I'll start with a slightly cheeky comment, which is, I think some of this is changing with the advent of large language models and the ability to actually just mimic someone else's tone. But I take inspiration from the camp of Anthony Bourdain, and he has, I'm going to butcher the exact quote but it's something like, "If you want to know how to make good food, you have to eat a lot of food, and you have to be willing to have a bad meal every now and again." And so for me, good writing comes from consuming as much good writing as possible. Sometimes you'll read something and say, "That was actually absolute fresh." But that's okay, you have to be willing to take on some of that stuff. But the more you index towards developing your own taste for what you think is good by consuming others, then you can shift into producing your own and then comparing them and riffing it off other people. So I think that's sort of the cycle that I've gone through.
turns.zh: 我先说个有点调侃的观点：随着大型语言模型的出现，以及模仿他人语气的能力增强，我觉得有些情况正在发生变化。但我深受安东尼·波登（Anthony Bourdain）理念的启发。他曾说过一句话——我可能记不太清原话了——大意是：“如果你想学会烹饪，就必须多品尝美食，偶尔也得接受糟糕的体验。” 对我而言，优秀的写作源于尽可能多地阅读优秀作品。有时读到某些内容会让人惊叹：“这真是天才之作！” 但没关系，你必须愿意接受这样的挑战。通过模仿他人的作品，逐渐形成自己的审美标准后，你才能开始创作并与他人交流灵感。这就是我走过的创作循环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a friend who's a very good writer and a poet and helped me develop my writing early on, Vanessa, and she said exactly the same thing. Just to become a better writer, read beautiful writing, and it just kind of infuses you or your brain. In your experience, is there anything you read, anything you found really effective? Anything that you think influenced the way you write or think that people can check out?
turns.zh: 我有个朋友叫瓦妮莎（Vanessa），她是个很棒的作家和诗人，早期帮我提升了写作水平。她也说过同样的话。想成为更好的作家，就去阅读优秀的作品，它们会潜移默化地影响你的大脑。以你个人的经验来看，有没有哪些作品特别有效？有没有影响你写作风格的作品，或者值得大家参考的作品？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I explicitly do not mean read a bunch of other PM artifacts. You're not going to become a better writer by reading PRDs or whatever it is or support articles. It needs to be writing that compels. That's the theme I would go back to because that's what you're trying to do at the end of the day. (00:16:56): And when I say compels, I mean it pushes you to action. Because if you read something and you're like, "Oh, that's interesting," that's not enough. You need to be able to give someone something that then allows them to do something differently. And so the things for me that have been best... Obviously there's all the Paul Graham essays, I think his writing is very succinct, very clear, that's not novel. I learned a lot by finding specific voices back in the day on Twitter, and it wasn't always what they were posting on Twitter, but if they wrote an essay or a post, that would be their crispus thinking. And so you can use these broadcast channels to find where their golden nuggets are, but then spend time with those instead and don't worry about all the additional noise that comes with it.
turns.zh: 我绝对不是说去读一堆项目管理文档（PM artifacts）。读PRD（产品需求文档）之类的文件，或者支持性文章，并不能真正提升写作水平。必须是能激发灵感的作品。这才是关键所在，因为归根结底，你的目标就是创造出有感染力的内容。（00:16:56）：我说的激发灵感，是指能推动你采取行动。读到某些内容时若只是感叹“哦，真有趣”，那还不够。你必须能给读者带来切实的启发，让他们有所行动。对我来说，最有价值的作品……比如保罗·格雷厄姆（Paul Graham）的文章，我觉得他的写作简洁明了，这并不新鲜。过去我在Twitter上发现一些独特的声音，他们的推文未必精彩，但如果他们写了一篇文章或帖子，那就是他们精妙的思想结晶。你可以通过这些信息渠道找到他们的精华之作，然后花时间深入研究，而不必被过多冗余信息分心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Paul Graham actually, you mentioned him, he has a great piece on how to become a good, that we'll link to, where basically his advice is, write the way you talk. Just keep it really simple and really regular. And so we'll link to that. Is there anything else along these lines of writing that you'd recommend for folks that are like, "Okay, I need to become a great writer. How do I do this?"?
turns.zh: 保罗·格雷厄姆确实很棒，你提到过他，他有一篇关于如何成为优秀作家的文章，我们会附上链接。他的核心建议是：写作要像说话一样自然，保持简洁流畅。我们会附上链接。对于那些想成为优秀作家的人，你还有什么推荐吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Actually along the lines of write how you talk, there's this concept of cadence that I think is really important when it comes to internal writing. There's probably some very good article about this, but it's the idea that if you only write in a monotonous cadence, either all really short sentences or all really long sentences, then your brain just tunes out eventually. And so you have to interrupt the pattern intentionally, and so you go short-long, long-short, whatever it is, but there's a few various specific things that you can do that allow someone to just roll through a post or something when you write that way.
turns.zh: 实际上，在“写作要像说话一样自然”这一理念的基础上，还有一个节奏感的概念，我认为这在内部写作中非常重要。可能有相关的优秀文章探讨过这个问题，但核心在于，如果你只用单调的语句结构——要么全是短句，要么全是长句——大脑最终会自动过滤掉这些内容。因此，你需要有意打破这种模式，形成短句与长句交替的节奏感，这样当读者阅读你的文章时，才不会感到枯燥乏味。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, there's a book that I just found to make sure I had the right title called Several Short Sentences About Writing that is really helpful along these lines. And the whole book is very short sentences and it teaches you to write very short sentences because once you're good at that, you can get better writing longer sentences. And so we'll link to that too. It's like a really good book that I have two copies around my house that I kind of poke at sometimes.
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，我刚找到一本名为《关于写作的几个短句》的书，书名本身就很贴切，内容也非常实用。这本书全部由短句组成，教你如何写出简洁有力的短句——因为一旦你掌握了这种技巧，再写长句时就会游刃有余。我们也会附上链接。这本书真是太棒了，我家里有两本，有时会翻看。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Nice. I'll have [inaudible 00:19:09] too.
turns.zh: 不错。我也想看看[00:19:09不可听清的内容]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Another area that you have a really clever insight into is how the PM role fits with engineering design. We've talked about this a little bit, but you have a really clever way of just thinking about how these roles interact and who's responsible for what. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 好的。另一个你见解独到的领域是产品经理（PM）与工程设计的协作。我们之前稍微谈过这个话题，但你对这两个角色如何互动，谁该负责什么，有着非常巧妙的见解。请详细讲讲。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: So this description came from writing PRDs at Square. I think there was a lot of confusion from my team specifically when I joined them. For what it's worth, it was new product line, three engineers, three designers, there was nothing but a slide deck.
turns.zh: 这个描述来自我在Square公司编写产品设计文档（PRD）的经历。我加入团队时，他们对PRD的理解存在很多困惑。值得一提的是，当时那是一个新产品线，三个工程师、三个设计师，除了一份幻灯片，几乎没有其他资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Three engineers and three designers?
turns.zh: 三个工程师和三个设计师？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: The best ratio ever. This is a whole other thing. Most people, I would say, under invest in design, point-blank. When you get to a certain scale, maybe things change, but truly I don't think most teams have experienced what it feels like to have a really high design ratio and what that actually does to the quality of the work and the quality of the thinking. So shout out to designers. We need more, is the short version. And I would rather hire an incremental designer than PM almost any day of the week.
turns.zh: 这简直是最理想的比例了。完全是另一个层面的问题。坦白说，我认为大多数团队在设计方面投入不足。当公司规模达到一定程度时，情况可能会有所改善，但说实话，我不认为大多数团队真正体验过高设计比例对工作质量和思维质量的提升。所以向设计师致敬吧。简而言之，我们需要更多设计师。几乎每个星期我都更愿意招聘一名额外的设计师，而不是产品经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I've never experienced this ratio. Incredible.
turns.zh: 哇。我从未经历过这样的比例。太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Yes, I was very lucky. Shout out to Bruce Bell, who was my manager at the time, who was an ex designer, at the time, GM, and declared that starting ratio. (00:20:31): So anyways, with that setup, they all had sort of an opinion. They had seen PRDs in the past, they weren't quite sure what the purpose of it actually was because they had designs already. They had something to start from. And when I came in and talked to everyone and figured out where we needed to be in a year's time, I was like, "Okay, here's how I think it. Let me know if you agree." And this is a whole other concept, which is, the best way to get feedback from people is not by asking what they think, but to put something concrete in front of them and then have them react to it, right? So chewing fork. (00:21:03): And so my description is, PM should be doing everything in their power to draw the perimeter of the space, of the problem space. And it's within that, eng, design, everyone else that you're working with, they can go as crazy as they want, push up against the bounds and it's fill the box to its maximum capacity, but you've now applied the constraints that allow you to actually have productive conversations. (00:21:26): On the other end of the spectrum though, I think there's a lot of folks who think, "Oh, PMs are just strategy high in the clouds. All they do is kick things off." You need to be obsessed about the final deliverable and whether or not value is actually getting to the customer. I have a really trite example of this if you want to go down it.
turns.zh: 是的，我运气确实很好。要感谢当时我的经理布鲁斯·贝尔，他曾是一名设计师，后来转任总经理，正是他提出了那个初始比例。（00:20:31）总之，基于这样的架构，每个人都有自己的看法。他们过去看过PRD文档，但不太清楚其用途，因为他们手头已经有设计方案，有现成的起点。当我加入团队后，和大家沟通并明确了未来一年的目标时，我说：“好吧，我是这么想的，如果你们有不同意见随时提出来。”这其实是另一个思路——获取反馈的最佳方式不是询问他们的看法，而是先拿出具体方案，让他们根据实际情况作出回应。比如用餐叉的例子。（00:21:03）我认为产品经理应该全力以赴划定问题的边界。在这个框架内，工程、设计以及其他合作伙伴可以尽情发挥，突破边界，充分挖掘潜力，但前提是先设定了能促进有效沟通的约束条件。（00:21:26）不过另一方面，很多人认为“产品经理不过是高高在上的战略制定者，除了启动项目什么都不做”。你必须专注于最终交付成果，确保价值真正传递到客户手中。如果你感兴趣，我可以举个老生常谈的例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 请继续。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: But the key point I want to make is, I think it is tempting when we think about engineering product and design to draw these really clear swim lanes and say, "You do X. I do Y. Don't tread on my area." But you need these murky overlaps in order to build something really good. (00:22:07): And so even if the engineers are going to build a better product than you and the designers are going to design something better than you, you need to come with a strong opinion and you need to do the legwork to get their trust so they actually care about your opinion in the first place. (00:22:21): So time for a mini story. So Square, we're building a point of sale for restaurants. If you've ever seen one of these in a restaurant, there's this sort of grid of tiles that they tap to enter your order when you're sitting down for dinner. We were developing one, and there's this concept of a menu group. So it's a little box, you tap on it and then it pops the screen in so you go to the next level of the hierarchy. So example would be you have a wine button, you tap it, and you see your reds, whites, et cetera. (00:22:53): If you think about the people that we were trying to serve, there's the restaurants that were coming from a really old legacy system. And if you've seen a bartender tap on one of these, I mean it is muscle memory to the max. They're not even looking at the thing and just punching in the order blindfolded, and it's rapid fast. (00:23:12): On the other hand, you have people who are entering the workforce the first time, they've never used a point of sale. And so we have to serve both of these equally. Well, how do you deal with that level of speed but also the ease of use that anyone can learn it for the first time? And so there was this interaction that we really cared about, which was, when you tap on a menu group, what's the animation to pop you into that next level? This seems like such a small thing, but it made the difference in how easy it was to adopt for a lot of the restaurants. (00:23:41): And so a designer and myself spent literally an entire week just fine-tuning how many milliseconds it would take to pop in and out so that it felt right. And we actually brought in servers and bartenders to play with the prototypes we had on iPads and be like, "Here's an order. Pop it in." And we would see where they would sort of flinch or hesitate because the animation was too slow and they thought, "I can't tap it yet," or something related to that. (00:24:07): And so it's easy, I think, for a PM to say, "That's not my responsibility. I define the requirements. Have a menu group that goes to the next level, design or engineer, figure it out." No way. That's fully on you, and you better be involved in those details.
turns.zh: 但我想强调的关键点是，当我们思考工程产品和设计时，往往会倾向于划分清晰的职责范围，说：“你负责X，我负责Y，别越界。” 但要打造出真正优秀的产品，就需要模糊的职责重叠区。（00:22:07） 即便工程师能比你开发出更优质的产品，设计师能设计出更出色的方案，你也必须提出强有力的观点，并通过耐心沟通赢得他们的信任，这样他们才会真正重视你的意见。（00:22:21） 接下来讲个小故事。Square公司当时在开发餐厅点餐系统。大家应该见过餐厅里的那种触摸屏界面——顾客就座后，通过点击一排网格按钮输入订单。我们设计了一个菜单组功能，即一个小方块，点击后会弹出子菜单。比如，用户点击葡萄酒按钮，就能看到红葡萄酒、白葡萄酒等分类。（00:22:53） 我们的用户群体一方面是来自传统遗留系统的老牌餐厅，这些员工操作起来如同肌肉记忆，闭着眼就能快速下单；另一方面是初入职场的新人，对点餐系统一无所知。我们必须同时兼顾两类用户需求。如何在保证操作速度的同时，让新手也能轻松上手？我们特别关注菜单组弹出动画效果。这看似微不足道的细节，却决定了餐厅的接受程度。（00:23:41） 设计师和我花了整整一周时间优化弹出速度，最终确定毫秒级动效最合适。甚至请来服务员和调酒师在iPad原型机上实际操作，观察他们是否会因动画太慢而犹豫不决。（00:24:07） 产品经理或许会说：“这不是我的责任。我负责定义需求，设计或工程团队会处理。” 不行！这完全是你的职责，你必须深入参与每个细节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. There's two directions I want to go. So there's the drawing the perimeter, and then there's this paying attention to the final deliverable and keeping the borrow really high, which I love and I totally agree with both. (00:24:34): In terms of this animation, people hearing this, that our PMs are going to be like, "How do you have time to spend a week on animation for one little product? I have so much to do. I get to hit some goals, drive some numbers. I have people waiting for me." Maybe because Square is like this, once you deploy, it's harder to change and it's like a big deal to ship. But I'm curious if you have any advice or things you've learned about how to create space for that sort of thing to create time to spend a week on this animation? Or was it just obvious to everyone, "We need to spend as much time as we can"? Top down, everyone knew.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。我有两个想发展的方向。一是设计产品边界，二是注重最终交付成果，同时保持高标准的借款体验。这两点我都非常赞同和认同。（00:24:34）：说到这个动画，可能听众会觉得我们的项目经理会说：“你怎么有时间花一周时间做一个小产品的动画？我有太多事情要做。我要达成目标、提升数据，还有人等着我呢。”也许是因为Square的架构一旦上线就很难更改，发布产品就像件大事。但我很好奇，你们有没有什么建议或经验，如何为这类事情腾出时间？还是说大家都觉得“我们必须尽可能多花时间”？从上到下，每个人都心知肚明。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I definitely don't think it was obvious to everyone, and I can definitely say that because we were given a pretty strict deadline that we needed to launch by and I pushed it out three times. That's not because of this one animation, but it's because of a series of decisions where we said, "This is what we believe we need to ship, and this matters much more than hitting some artificial external GA date." (00:25:35): There's this other aspect that I think PMs like to feel good about how busy they are and they're like, "I'm involved in so many processes and I have to talk to this person and talk to that person." All that might be true, but I think there needs to be a calibration or at least a spring-cleaning of, "What's everything I'm doing?" and how much do these things actually matter to getting value to a customer. Because as a company gets bigger, as teams get more complex, it's very easy and natural to spend more time on things that are internally-focused and not externally-focused. I think we just all have to have sensitive antenna to that so that we don't fall prey to, "Well, the way that my job is described is to do these things," but really it's the outcome again of put something in a customer's hands that's also a problem, and it's amazing.
turns.zh: 我绝对不认为这对每个人来说都是显而易见的。我可以肯定地说，因为我们被赋予了一个非常严格的发布期限，我已经三次推迟了。这不只是因为这个动画，而是因为一系列决策。我们说：“这是我们认为必须推出的产品，这比达成某些人为设定的外部目标日期重要得多。”（00:25:35）：我认为还有另一个方面，就是项目经理们喜欢标榜自己有多忙，他们会说：“我参与了太多流程，还要和这个人沟通、和那个人沟通。” 这些或许都是事实，但我认为需要进行校准或至少进行一次“大扫除”，审视自己正在做的一切事务。这些事情对为客户创造价值到底有多重要？随着公司规模扩大、团队复杂度增加，很容易自然而然地把更多时间花在内部关注的事情上，而不是外部关注的事情上。我认为我们都需要对此保持敏锐的觉察，避免陷入“嗯，我的职责描述就是做这些事情”的陷阱，而真正关键的还是要把产品交到客户手中，这才是问题所在，真是令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reminds me of your now colleague Jeff Weinstein's advice he got from one of the Coulsons where they came to him and they're like, "You're world-class at doing the second and third most important things and you're not focusing on the most important thing because it's so hard, and that's something you need to work on."
turns.zh: 这让我想起你现在的同事杰夫·温斯坦从库尔森那里得到的建议。他们找到他，说：“你在做第二和第三重要的事情方面是世界级的，但你没有专注于最重要的事情，因为那太难了，这方面你需要改进。”

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally. I will say so one on that, the CEO at Mutiny, Charlie, she always repeated to me nonstop, "Keep the main thing the main thing" and would just say it ad nauseum, and I'm really glad that she did. The one excuse I don't want to give folks is, as you progress in your career, you have to walk and chew gum at the same time. You can't say, "Oh, I'm only focused on this thing over here, so other folks handle that." You do have to figure out how to do a little bit more at the same time, but prioritization does play a factor.
turns.zh: 完全同意。我要就此说一句，Mutiny的CEO查理总是不断对我说：“把最重要的事情放在最重要位置”，说到让人厌烦的地步。我真的很庆幸她这么做了。我不想给人们一个借口，说“随着职业生涯发展，你必须一心二用”。你不能说：“哦，我只专注于这边的事情，其他让别人处理吧。”你确实需要想办法同时多做一点事，但优先级确实很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a framework [inaudible 00:27:27] suggested that I really like, the LNO framework. I forget exactly what the LNO stands for, but leverage something something. And we'll link to it in the show notes that gives you some advice on how to prioritize your time based on the stuff.
turns.zh: 有一个框架[00:27:27听不清]，我很喜欢，叫LNO框架。我忘了LNO具体代表什么，但借助一些东西。我们会在节目笔记中附上链接，里面有一些基于时间优先级的建议。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So I guess in the case of pushing back to create space, this was just you as a product leader recognizing, "This is really important to get right. I will convince people we need to make more time for that."
turns.zh: 好的。所以我猜在推迟进度以腾出空间的情况下，这只是你作为产品负责人，意识到“这件事必须做好，必须说服大家为此腾出更多时间”。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I don't want to make it seem like it was me against everyone because that was definitely not the case. I think the starting engineers and designers on that team really cared about the quality of what they built too. That's a pretty structural DNA for a team as well. If you don't start with that, and as a comparison, you have a team that really prides themselves on shipping fast and meeting deadlines really prescriptively, you might end up in a different world or your role as a PM might be a little bit more challenging if you want to push on this stuff. So I do think you have to take into account what is the DNA of the team. And then can you exploit that? Which I was able to do. Or do you actually have some change management to put into effect if you believe that it's worthwhile?
turns.zh: 我不想让人觉得我是在和所有人对抗，因为事实绝非如此。我认为那个团队的初级工程师和设计师也非常重视他们所开发产品的质量。这也是一个团队的结构性特质。如果你没有从一开始就树立这种理念，而相比之下，如果有一个团队过分强调快速交付、死板执行截止日期，那么当你想推动这些事情时，可能会面临截然不同的处境。因此，我确实认为你必须考虑团队的文化特质。然后，你能否加以利用？我当时就做到了。或者，如果你认为这值得去做，是否需要实施一些变革管理措施？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's go back to the perimeter, drawing the perimeter concept to make that a little more real for people. So your advice here is the role of a PM, part of your main job, especially when it comes to engineers and design is to draw the perimeter for the team. Can you make that a little more real? What's an example of that maybe from something you worked on? What does that look like?
turns.zh: 让我们回到“边界”的概念，让这个概念更具实际意义。所以你在这里的建议是，产品经理的角色，特别是对工程师和设计师来说，就是为团队划定边界。你能否再具体点说明？或许可以举个你参与过的项目的例子？这具体是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally. The best word to describe the perimeter is just constraints. At the end of the day, you should be adding as many constraints as reasonable in order to let engineers and designers come up with the most creative solutions for whatever you're trying to do. (00:29:15): And so again, if we just stay focused on this point of sale example, one constraint would be, "Who the hell are we serving? Are we trying to go after sit-down restaurants that are serving five different courses and have a 200 item wine list? Or are we trying to serve the taco truck?" Those will lead to very different spaces. And if you leave both on the table, the lack of that constraint makes designing a good solution that much harder, that there instances where you actually can't apply that many constraints. But I bet that if you push on enough different axes, you eventually scope it down to a point where it feels really good for the team. It's just about how do you remove decisions, right? Because this I think is maybe a trite phrase, but the best decision is no decision. If you don't even have to think about the decision, the team is that much more effective.
turns.zh: 完全正确。描述边界的最佳词汇就是约束条件。归根结底，你应该合理地增加尽可能多的约束条件，让工程师和设计师为你要实现的目标想出最具创造性的解决方案。（00:29:15）：再以销售点示例为例，一个约束条件可能是：“我们到底要服务谁？是那些提供五道菜、拥有200种酒类清单的堂食餐厅？还是只做塔可餐车？”这两者会带来截然不同的市场空间。如果你两者都兼顾，缺乏这种约束条件会让设计出好的解决方案变得极其困难。当然，有时候你确实无法施加太多约束条件。但我敢打赌，如果你在多个维度上持续推进，最终会将范围缩小到让团队感觉非常舒适的程度。这其实就是如何消除决策的过程，对吧？因为我觉得这句话听起来可能有些老生常谈，但最好的决策就是不做决策。如果你甚至无需考虑这个决策，团队的效率就会大大提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So yo give people a few maybe even pointers of, "I need to create more constraints maybe for my team to help them go crazy, but within this box that we all agree on," so you mentioned make sure the user's clear of who you're designing for. Is there anything else, just thinking about maybe the PRD someone's trying to write to help create this constraint? What other maybe bullet points, sections would you imagine or do you find useful to add?
turns.zh: 所以你给人们一些建议，比如：“我需要为我的团队创建更多约束条件，让他们在我们都认可的框架内尽情发挥创造力。”你提到的要确保用户清楚你为谁设计。还有其他方面吗？比如有人正在努力撰写PRD来帮助建立这个约束条件？你还能想到哪些要点或有用的部分可以添加？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: So beyond customer segment/like-what-their-specific-role is, I think another one would be, we can loosely call it, jobs to be done, even though I know that's becoming an increasingly loaded term.
turns.zh: 所以除了客户细分/明确他们的特定角色之外，我认为还有一个可以松散地称之为“待完成的工作”的维度，尽管我知道这个术语正变得越来越有争议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's great.
turns.zh: 是的，这很棒。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: But what's the thing they're trying to do and how many different pathways are you willing to entertain around it? That's another one that I would think about. Depending on what you're building, there's availability. So do you care about desktop web, mobile web, native mobile, et cetera? And maybe another one to think through just as an example would be, this is probably getting closer to what a lot of people think about in terms of principles, but what are the things that you want to be known for when you ship a product? One example there might be speed. And so if you say speed is more important than consistency of data, that's a huge tradeoff and constraint that you can give the team." Oh my god, if an engineer hears I don't need real time consistency of data, I can do so much cool stuff and easily accomplish that speed thing." And so that's just a very technical example maybe.
turns.zh:
好的，但他们想做的是什么？你愿意考虑多少种不同的实现路径？这是我会思考的另一个问题。取决于你正在开发的产品，有哪些可用的方案。那么你是否关心桌面网页、移动网页、原生移动应用等？再举个例子，虽然这可能更接近于人们在原则层面所考虑的问题，但当你推出产品时，你希望以什么为特色呢？比如速度。假如你说速度比数据一致性更重要，那这就是一个巨大的权衡和约束，你得向团队说明这一点。

“天哪，如果工程师听到‘我不需要实时数据一致性’，他们会想‘我可以做很多酷炫的事，轻松实现速度目标’。”这只是个技术层面的例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, I'm glad I followed up on that. There's a couple more things you mentioned that I want to come back to real quick. The first is this tuning fork idea. I completely agree, this point you made, that the best way to get feedback from your team is to take a first pass at it, and here's a rough quick draft. I find with design, especially if you design something ugly, designers are often like, "Let me make that better. We can't stand this thing." Is there anything else you want to add there? Just this idea of tuning fork as a feedback strategy.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我很高兴能跟进这个问题。你提到的另外两个方面我也想快速回顾一下。第一个是关于“音叉”（Tuning Fork）的反馈策略。我完全赞同你的观点——让团队提供反馈的最佳方式就是先做一个初稿，然后拿出一份粗略的快速草案。我发现设计方面尤其如此，尤其是当设计出来的东西不够美观时，设计师们往往会说：“让我改进一下，这个方案我们实在无法忍受。” 你还有什么要补充的吗？特别是关于“音叉”作为反馈策略的想法。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Okay, there's two areas we can go deeper on here. One is in how you get the feedback. So this is definitely a Square-ism, I think it was probably adopted from Amazon, which is around the silent read of documents. When you are all so busy and someone's like, "I wrote a doc," you send it into the Slack ecosystem and everyone goes, "Please give feedback." You have so much going on... You'll be lucky to maybe get a response. Maybe there's one or two people that chime in. (00:32:35): And so even though we hate meetings and we love asynchronous, there is a lot of value to saying, "I need 20 minutes of focused time to interrogate something that I've done. We're not going to talk. I'm literally going to force us into a room or Zoom. You're going to read this doc, I'm going to watch you comment on it in real time. I'm going to respond to your comments in real time. And at the end of this thing I'm going to have enough really good input that I can do a huge rub on this thing and get to the next phase."
turns.zh: 好的，这里有两个可以深入探讨的方面。第一个是如何获取反馈。这绝对是Square的做法，我认为它可能源自亚马逊的做法，即对文档进行“静默阅读”。当大家都很忙碌，有人发送文档时，大家会把它发送到Slack平台，然后大家会说：“请提供反馈。” 但你有太多事情要处理……能得到回复就已经很幸运了，可能只有一两个人会参与讨论。（00:32:35）所以尽管我们讨厌开会、喜欢异步沟通，但安排20分钟的专注时间来审视自己做过的东西，效果会好很多。我们不讨论，只是一起进入会议室或Zoom会议，让大家实时评论文档，我也会实时回应评论。最后，我们会获得足够好的反馈，可以对产品进行重大改进，进入下一阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. So it's basically instead of, "Hey, I'm sending you this doc to go review, give me feedback," it's, "I'm going to schedule a meeting, and the meeting is for you to spend time reviewing this doc and giving me feedback and then maybe we could talk about it."
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种方式。不是“嘿，我把文档发给你去审阅，请给我反馈”，而是“我要安排一个会议，专门让你们花时间审阅文档并提供反馈，然后我们再讨论。”

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Yep. And I think a lot of people are going to hate hearing that because like, "Oh my god, I have so many meetings already. Why do I want another meeting that isn't even a meeting?" But that's the best kind then, because it's actual work getting done, right? And maybe you carve out two minutes at the end for one really immediate discussion topic or something. But I don't think we give enough space in any type of meeting for people to actually think. And when you are just staring at a doc with your camera off and the only expectation is to engage with that thing, thoughts are a little bit better and crisper.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为很多人会讨厌这种做法，因为他们会想：“天哪，我已经开会太多了。为什么还要开另一个根本不算会议的会议？” 但这才是最好的会议类型，因为这是实实在在的工作成果，对吧？也许最后可以留出两分钟时间讨论一个紧急议题之类的。但我认为我们在任何类型的会议中都没有给人们足够的空间去真正思考。当你关掉摄像头，专注于文档时，唯一的期望就是参与讨论，思路会更清晰、更敏捷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think with this idea, if someone says, "I want a meeting where you just sit and review this doc," you could always say, "Let me just review it asynchronously. I'll give you feedback, I promise. Give me 24 hours." Right? It's not like they have to come to this meeting.
turns.zh: 我认为基于这个思路，如果有人说：“我希望开个会，你就坐下来审阅这份文档。”你可以回应：“让我异步审阅一下吧。我会给你反馈的，保证24小时内完成。”对吧？反正他们又不一定要来这个会议。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Although I would urge you to make them come to the meeting.
turns.zh: 不过我还是建议你让他们来参加会议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, say more there, because you find that that's a lot more effective.
turns.zh: 好的，再多说几句，因为你发现这样更有效。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I think there's two sneaky things hiding behind that. One is the, "Yeah, I'll get to this in the next 24 hours." Maybe they don't. Maybe you've really trust that person and they're the exception. But beyond that, there is something else to the real time interaction that can happen when you're commenting and responding on a dock at the same time. I think this is the part that often gets lost, which is the latency between a comments or question and a quick follow-up from the author just pushes that cycle speed really long in a way that doesn't need to be. And so when people are trying to find how do you move faster, this actually is one of those very good examples of moving slower to move faster.
turns.zh: 我觉得这背后有两个隐藏的隐患。第一种情况是：“嗯，我24小时内处理。”但他们可能做不到。也许你真的很信任这个人，所以他们是个例外。但除此之外，实时互动也很重要——当你在文档上同时评论和回复时，互动效果会更好。这一点常被忽视，因为从提出问题到作者快速回复之间的延迟会导致整个反馈周期过长，没有必要如此拖沓。所以当人们在寻找如何提高效率时，放慢节奏反而能加速进程，这就是个很好的例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me Claire Vo, I think it was her phrase of moving one clock speed faster, and just like that's the way you speed up a company is try to move one clock speed faster, which in this case is just reduce the time between feedback and iteration. I love it. (00:35:13): Okay, I want to shift to talking about a few very tactical things that you've found really helpful in your PM career and something you recommend to other product teams. The first is something you call a decision log. You think every PM should keep a decision log. Talk about what that is and why that's powerful.
turns.zh:
这让我想起Claire Vo，她提过“加快一个时钟节拍”的说法。就像加速公司发展要比别人快一个节拍一样，在这种情况下，就是缩短反馈和迭代之间的周期。我很认同这个观点。
（00:35:13）好的，接下来我想聊聊你在产品经理生涯中发现的几个实用的技巧，以及你给其他产品团队的建议。第一个是所谓的“决策日志”。你认为每个产品经理都应该保留决策日志。请解释一下这是什么，以及它为何如此有效。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I will say there's two different decision logs we could talk about. We'll focus on the former though. The latter is just as you're making decisions within your job, you should document those within a PRD. Make sure everyone knows. It's just a silly, very small thing, but I think every PM should do it. (00:35:48): The other decision log though that I think is quite critical is if we zoom out for a second, every person has something that they can do to slightly increment in their craft. Sprinters have certain exercises that they do. There's something beautiful about pianists and piano scales where it doesn't matter if you are just learning the piano or you are a 30-year veteran, you're still doing your scales, and it's because it lays the foundation for everything else that you need to do. (00:36:23): And so we all talk about product sense. It's this super mystical thing that no one knows how to get better at. To me, it's just a fancy way of saying you can make good decisions with insufficient data, and the core of that is decisions. And so PMs need as many reps as possible in making decisions, documenting the rationale behind those decisions, and then crucially seeing the outcome of them. And so the natural followup would be, "Well, I only have to make X decisions in my job. How the hell do I make more of them?" Look around you. There's other teams that are making decisions. What would you do if you were in that position with the information you have? Great, write it down. Say why. (00:37:06): There's other companies that are doing crazy things. What are they doing? What would you do if you were responsible for the roadmap? Write it down. A year later, see what they've shipped. You can just do this for anyone. It's free, and no one takes the time to do it, but that's how I think you get better at actually making decisions, is just doing more of them.
turns.zh: 我要说的是，我们可以讨论两种不同的决策记录。不过我们今天主要关注前者，后者就是在工作中做决策时，你应该把这些记录在PRD（产品需求文档）里，让所有人都能看到。这看似是件微不足道的小事，但我认为每个产品经理都应该这么做。（00:35:48）不过另一种决策记录更重要，如果我们退后一步看，每个人都可以通过一些方法来微微提升自己的专业技能。短跑运动员有特定的训练项目。钢琴家练习音阶这件事很美妙——无论你是刚学琴的新手，还是有30年经验的老手，都要坚持练习，因为它为你后续的所有工作奠定了基础。（00:36:23）我们常谈论“产品洞察力”，但这似乎是个神秘的东西，很多人不知道如何提升。在我看来，这不过是说在数据不足的情况下也能做出明智决策，而决策的核心在于执行力。因此，产品经理需要尽可能多地练习决策，记录决策背后的逻辑，并关键性地观察决策结果。接下来自然会产生疑问：“但我的工作中只有X个决策机会啊，怎么才能增加决策次数呢？”看看身边的团队，他们在做决策时，你会怎么做？把想法写下来。再想想其他公司在大胆尝试，他们在做什么？如果你负责路线图规划，又会如何决策？把思路记录下来。一年后再看看他们的成果。这些练习适用于任何人。免费又简单，但没人愿意花时间去做，但我认为这正是提升决策能力的关键——就是多做决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hearing you describe this, it feels like, "Obviously yes, why aren't we doing this? How else can we get better if we're not reflecting back on the decisions we've made? And realizing, "Hey, I made a bunch of bad decisions, but I'm always so confident in my decision still, maybe shouldn't be. So I guess first of all, do you actually do this? How often do you do this? And is there an example of you learning something from your own decision log?
turns.zh: 听你这么描述，感觉就像：“显然应该这么做啊，为什么我们不这么做呢？如果不反思已有的决策，又怎么能进步呢？然后意识到，‘哎呀，我做过很多糟糕的决策，但我每次都那么自信，或许不该这样。’所以首先，你自己真的会这么做吗？多久做一次？能举个例子说明从决策记录中学到了什么吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Many. And many of them because it was a wrong decision. But yes, I do keep a decision log. I have a separate sort of practice where it's just a daily log, which is everyone wants the perfect note-taking system. To me, the best note-taking system is inspired by... What is it called? big ass text file, BATF. There's a funny blog post from 2001 on it, but it's just, you write everything that happens to you in a day in a bolded list and it's all in one big note. That way you can command F it, do whatever you want. The way that I keep track of it is I do a little hashtag decision and then write things down just as I think about them. And then I'll have a reminder to comb back through on some cadence. (00:38:36): And so I'll first use a positive example, which is a funny one. So if you rewind to, I don't even know what year, but Shopify had just launched Shop app, their consumer application for what started as tracking your order when you bought something from a Shopify customer and then it's evolved into a full-blown Amazon competitor, where you can actually find merchants and buy things through it. (00:39:03): When they first launched it though, I was like, "Oh my God, this is so brilliant. They have completely hijacked this specific loop for consumer buying behavior via this very unassuming thing, which is package tracking." And so that morning I was like, "Whatever, I'm going to quickly draw a diagram of this flywheel that I think Amazon owns today. I'm going to show how Shopify is slowly planting their little seed to take over this and how Shop app fits into it." I tweeted out. And then I don't know, that day there must have been 60 Shopify employees that followed me. I was like, "What the hell is this guy talking about?" (00:39:40): And so funny enough, fast-forward, I've talked to some of the folks that worked on it and they're like, "Yeah, nailed it. Here's what we were thinking. Here's why." It's no longer secret sauce. But that was a really interesting example of both doing a decision log, putting my rationale down on paper. In this case, broadcasting it out, but then having that be a mechanism for it making its way back to me to actually better understand why did they make the decision versus what I thought, because the reasons were a little bit different, but the outcome was the same. So that's one interesting example.
turns.zh:
很多啊，其中很多是因为做出了错误的决定。不过没错，我确实会记录自己的决策过程。我还有个专门的日志习惯——每天把所有想法都写下来。毕竟每个人都想找到完美的笔记系统，但对我来说，最棒的笔记系统灵感来源于……叫什么来着？大文本文件（BATF）。2001年有篇关于它的搞笑博文，不过核心就是：你把一天经历写成加粗列表，全部收录在一个大笔记里。这样你就能随心所欲，根本无需在意后果。我现在记录的方式是先用#决策标签，然后随时把想法记下来。之后我会定期回顾提醒自己。

（00:38:36）先举个正面例子，挺有趣的。记得Shopify刚推出Shop app的时候（我都不记得具体年份了），他们的消费者应用最初是追踪在Shopify商户处下单的物流进度，后来逐渐演变成亚马逊的竞争对手——用户可以通过它搜索商家并购买商品。当时我特别兴奋：“天啊，这太妙了。他们通过一个看似不起眼的功能——包裹追踪，彻底颠覆了消费者的购买行为模式。”那天早上我兴致勃勃地画了张飞轮图，标注出亚马逊如今占据的市场份额，分析Shopify如何逐步布局接管这块领域，Shop app又如何完美契合。结果发推后，60个Shopify员工关注了我。我当时就想：“这家伙在说什么鬼话？”

（00:39:03）有趣的是，后续我和参与开发的团队交流，他们说：“太对了！我们当时就是这么想的。原因是……”。这不再是商业机密了。这个例子很好地说明了记录决策过程和将逻辑具象化的重要性。通过公开分享，你能反思决策背后的深层逻辑，发现真实动机与你的推测存在差异，最终优化决策效果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's an amazing story. You doing this explains why you've been so successful. I could see how this all connects now. I think for a lot of people, they would want to build this habit. Clearly there's a lot of value here, but they just don't because they got a lot of other things going on or it's just like this new thing they have to start doing. Is there anything that helped you adopt this practice of this daily log/decision log that you think might be helpful to folks to motivate them to give this a shot?
turns.zh: 这真是个精彩的故事。你的做法解释了你为何如此成功。我现在终于明白这一切如何串联起来了。我觉得很多人都想养成这种习惯。显然这里面有很多价值，但他们往往因为忙于其他事务，或者觉得这又是个需要强制执行的新任务而望而却步。有没有什么方法能帮助人们养成这种每日日志/决策日志的习惯，从而激励他们尝试一下？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: This is probably just general advice on building any habit, which is start small and just force yourself to do it. And there's that old saying around, how do you start running as a hobby? You don't do it by saying, "I'm going to run a mile every day." You do it by putting your sneakers at the foot of your bed unless you take your shoes off inside, then you put it at the front door, you have your shorts ready to go and you're like, "I commit to putting on my shorts. And if I decide after getting dressed to go run, that I still don't want to go run. Okay, fine." But you build up to that thing. (00:41:16): I think decision logs are the lightest weight thing possible. And so you can start super easy by saying, "You know what? Every Sunday morning I'm going to scroll through Twitter, I'm going to check out Hacker News, whatever it is, I'm going to see something interesting and I'm going to make a bet. I'm going to place my decision on this thing." Write it down, and then set a calendar invite in X weeks, X months to see what plays out. And that's all it is, right? 10 minutes once a week, super easy. And then over time you can crank it up. And then eventually you're just constantly writing these decisions down and then it's like feeding its way back into you. It becomes second nature.
turns.zh:
这可能只是关于养成任何习惯的一般性建议——从小处着手，强迫自己去做。还有一句老话：如何开始把跑步当作爱好呢？你不会一开始就说“我要每天跑一英里”。你会把运动鞋放在床脚（除非你在家不换鞋），然后放在前门，准备好短裤，心里想：“我决定穿上短裤。如果穿好衣服后还是不想去跑步，那就算了。” 但你会逐渐养成这个习惯。  
（00:41:16）我认为决策日志是成本最低的工具。你可以从最简单的事情开始，比如：“每周日早上，我会浏览推特、查看 Hacker News 之类的平台，看到感兴趣的内容后下个赌注。” 把这个想法写下来，然后在 X 周、X 个月后设置日历提醒，看看结果如何。这真的很简单，每周花10分钟时间。随着时间推移，你可以逐渐增加频率。最终，你会习惯不断记录这些决策，它们会自然融入你的日常思维，成为第二天性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're touching on something that there's been a little bit of talk on this podcast and newsletter post about this idea of to get better product sense and product taste and also just decision making this case, one of the best strategies is to simulate other people's decisions and simulate what they're thinking through and predict what they're going to do, which is what you're describing here.
turns.zh: 你提到的观点在播客和新闻通讯中也被多次讨论过——要提高产品敏锐度和品味，尤其是在决策方面，最好的策略之一就是模拟他人的决策过程，预测他们的行为。这正是你在这里描述的做法。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally. I do want to apply a pretty severe caveat here though, which is, a decision log is not a replacement for building products. It's a additional complimentary thing that you can be doing on your own. But if you think that you can just sit back in your chair, look out at the market, make a bunch of calls and be like, "Look at how smart I'm getting without actually being hands-on with building a product," you're not actually going to get any better. So I just want to interject that
turns.zh: 完全同意。不过我要强调一点：决策日志不能替代产品开发。这只是你可以自主实践的辅助工具。但如果你以为坐在椅子上观察市场、打几个电话就能自诩聪明，却不亲自参与产品开发，那你永远无法真正提升自己。所以我要提醒大家：

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing caveat, very important. Don't just sit and read Hacker News and think you're going to be become an amazing founder or product leader.
