Say decision log or daily log, is it just things that happen today and then hashtag, "Here's a decision I made, or here's a decision I think Shopify will make in the future"? Is that the format?
turns.zh: 太棒了，这点提醒非常重要。别只是坐着看Hacker News，幻想自己能成为出色的创始人或产品负责人。（00:42:49）本期节目由Eppo赞助。Eppo是一款由Airbnb和Snowflake前员工为现代增长团队打造的下一代A/B测试和功能管理平台。Twitch、Miro、ClickUp和DraftKings等公司都依赖Eppo来推动实验。（00:43:05）实验对推动增长和了解新功能表现愈发重要。Eppo帮助您提升实验速度，同时通过先进的统计方法实现严谨的深度分析，这是其他商业工具无法比拟的。我在Airbnb时，最怀念的就是我们的实验平台——我可以轻松设置实验、排除故障并分析效果，所有这些工作都能自己完成。Eppo通过先进的统计方法实现这一切，甚至更多：它能帮助您缩短实验周期，提供易用的界面深入分析性能，以及开箱即用的报告功能，助您避免冗长、耗时的分析循环。（00:43:42）Eppo还能让您轻松与团队分享实验见解，激发A/B测试良性循环的灵感。Eppo支持所有场景下的实验，包括产品、增长、机器学习、变现和邮件营销。访问get eppo.com/lenny，提升实验速度十倍。（00:44:07）如果有人想尝试每日日志的想法，具体该怎么做？比如决策日志或每日日志，是只记录今天发生的事然后加个标签吗？“这是我今天做的决定”或者“我认为Shopify未来会推出Shop App”？是这种格式吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Yeah, it depends on how far you want to go down productivity and notetaking as to rabbit holes, but let's start basic. This is not what I do, but I think it's the easiest place to start. Spin up a Google doc or a Notion page, just call it daily log and then bullet point out the date of today. And then as you're going through your day, you have a meeting, just type in the meeting name. If there's a takeaway, put it under there. If there's a decision you can make, do hashtag decision. And in this case, say, "Shopify launch Shop app. I think this is their way to take over the fulfillment to buying behavior loop. The reason for that is X, Y, Z." Follow up on this in six months and then set your calendar invite.
turns.zh: 对，这取决于你想在生产力和笔记方面深入到什么程度，但先从基础开始。这不是我常做的，但我觉得这是最容易入门的地方。创建一个Google文档或Notion页面，取名为每日日志，然后用项目符号标出今天的日期。接下来在一天中参加会议时，直接输入会议名称。如果有收获，就写在那里。如果有你能做的决定，就用标签“决策”。比如，“Shopify推出Shop app。我认为这是他们接管从下单到购买行为闭环的方式。原因是X、Y、Z。”六个月后再回顾，然后设置日程提醒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So as motivation for listeners to try this sort of thing, just look at the success Kevin has had as in his career and how insightful he has been so far and will continue to be. And this is how these happen. This is how your mind learns to see things in a really unique, interesting way. So I know you're modest and aren't going to take any credit, but I'm just saying this is how you get better, is trying stuff like this.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以为了激励听众尝试这种做法，看看Kevin在职业生涯中取得的成功，以及他迄今为止和将来会继续展现的洞察力。这就是成功的秘诀。这就是你的大脑如何学会以独特、有趣的方式看待事物。所以我知道你很谦虚，不想居功，但我只想说，这就是你进步的方式——尝试这样的新事物。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Footnote, correlation versus causation. It's all put out there.
turns.zh: 附注：相关性与因果关系。一切都摆在台面上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Could be all genes. Could be completely unrelated to anything you've done entire life, I suspect.
turns.zh: 可能全是基因问题。可能与你一生所做的一切毫无关联，我这么猜的。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Could just be me being very lucky, I'll put that out there.
turns.zh: 可能只是我运气好，我先这么说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Could also be luck. Okay, so something I wanted to touch on with this decision log idea, and it's a segue to talking about hiring, is I think interviewing is also really good opportunity to try some like this. I feel like people interview lots of people. They think they know what they're looking for. They think they've made all these decisions. They think they have these amazing interview questions that are going to help them see really good signal, but you never actually go back and see, "Was I right? Should we have hired that person? Did this person work out? Was that question asked them at all inform? Was it at all a leading indicator of anything?" And I feel like this is a really good method for improving your interviewing abilities, is like, "Here's the questions asked. Here's what I decided. Here's what I think," and then a year later look back, "Was that actually right?"
turns.zh: 也可能是运气。好的，关于这个决策日志的想法，我还想再深入探讨一下，这里顺便谈谈招聘问题。我觉得面试也是一个尝试类似方法的好机会。我发现很多人在面试候选人时，自以为很清楚自己在寻找什么样的人才，觉得自己已经做出了所有决策，还认为自己设计的面试问题能有效识别优秀人才，但事后却从不回头审视：“我的判断是否正确？我们本该录用那个人吗？那个人工作得如何？那个问题是否真的有价值？它是否预示着某种趋势？”我觉得通过这种方式来提升面试能力非常有效：先记录提问内容、自己的判断，再在一年后回头审视：“当初的决定是否明智？”

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Yeah, totally. I think some of the best companies actually do have a practice around this where they have a 6, 12, 18 month check-in on new hires and they then compare their performance against level hired at and then review against the scorecards. It's a pretty laborious process. So startups aren't probably going to do it in the same amount of rigor, but it shows you so much about the holes in your interviewing process. So I definitely plus one of that one.
turns.zh: 是啊，我完全赞同。我认为一些优秀的公司确实有这样的做法，他们会对新员工进行6个月、12个月、18个月的跟进评估，将他们的表现与同期入职者的表现进行比较，并对照评估标准进行复盘。这确实是个很繁琐的过程。所以初创公司可能没法做到同等的严谨度，但它能让你深刻认识到面试流程中的漏洞。我对这个做法绝对赞成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Oh my god, that puts all this pressure on your score, which is great. So that's actually a segue talking about hiring. There's a couple more tactics that I've seen you be really good at. So one is just hiring in general. You have a lot of interesting approaches to hiring, including this idea of a unsell email where you try to convince someone not to join your company. Talk about that and why you think that's effective and then anything else along the lines of hiring you've learned.
turns.zh: 太棒了。天哪，这会给你的评分带来巨大压力，但这正是好事。那我们接着聊聊招聘问题。你还有一些很棒的招聘策略。比如“反向推销邮件”这种方法，你会主动说服别人别来你的公司。能谈谈这个策略吗？为什么你觉得它有效？还有其他你学到的招聘技巧也欢迎分享。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I'll say the idea of the unsell email came from a place of failure, which is at Square I had shifted into a position where I had to hire a lot of people really quickly. And through that, as a fairly new hiring manager, you're like, "All right, great. I've been told the goal is to hire fast." Okay, you give me a metric, you're going to go after it. So you do your best to get as many people in the door as possible. When you're talking to your recruiting partner, they're incentivized to increase pass through rates, offer to close rates, all these other things, and so they're like, "Yeah, this person's really good." And you listen. "Yeah, they are pretty good, aren't they?" Even though there's a sneaking suspicion that maybe they're not the right fit, but you move forward anyways. (00:47:54): So fast-forward, there's a few folks I bring on, and within six months they come to me and they're like, "This is not at all what I thought I was going to do. This is not the environment I thought I was going to walk into. You didn't warn me about this, that and the other. I feel terrible. How do I prevent this?" And the reason it's bad is not just because they feel surprised, but because then, either one, they decide to leave, two, they're not performing because it's not the right role or environment for them, or three, maybe the company is still good, but that role isn't. And so they immediately try to do internal mobility or something to another team, which then leaves you with the same hole. So all of those bad outcomes. [inaudible 00:48:37] "How do I prevent this?" Well, I just got to front load all the gnarly stuff they're going to find out in their first six months. (00:48:44): And so the practice I started developing is you go through the whole interview process. During that period, you're collecting all these little concerns, fears, anxieties that they're not explicitly saying, but they're definitely hinting at. You got to be pretty honest with yourself about which ones are real. But then when you get to offer stage, I send an email with no more than eight bullet points and I say all the terrible things that are probably going to reinforce their fears. I'm pretty candid about, "This is what it's like here." Maybe one example would be, "Hey, I'm a parent and I'm worried about work-life balance." Maybe they don't say that explicitly in the interview process, but you get a feeling for it. And I get that as a parent too. (00:49:31): So if I'm at a startup, I'll be really clear and I'll say, "You know what? We are a series A startup. We are pushing really hard at product-market fit. The expectation here is going to be that you're online at 10:00, that you can occasionally hop on a meeting on a Saturday or Sunday." And if you can tell them that upfront and they can read that whole email and still be equally excited to join, you find yourself an A+ hire. But if they read that and they're like," I don't know anymore," it's way better to say, "Great, this is not a good fit. Let's go our separate ways" than have them leave after six months. (00:50:08): When I first instituted this, I lost 30% of candidates at offer stage.
turns.zh:
我得说，那封"劝退邮件"的灵感源自一次失败的招聘经历。在Square公司时，我曾被迫在短时间内招聘大量员工。作为一个新手招聘经理，我当时听从上级指示，认为目标就是快速招人。在这种激励机制下，你会尽可能多地吸引候选人。当你与招聘伙伴沟通时，他们会用高通过率、成交率等数据来刺激你，于是你会听信他们的判断，说：“嗯，这个人确实不错。”然而内心深处总有种隐约的怀疑——或许他并不适合这个岗位或环境，但你还是继续推进。

（00:47:54）：时间快进，几位新入职员工在入职半年内找到我，抱怨说：“这完全不是我想象中的工作。环境与预期相差太远。你从未告知我这些风险，我该如何避免这种情况？”问题的根源不仅在于他们的失望，更在于：一、他们选择离职；二、因不适应岗位或环境而表现不佳；三、公司本身不错，但该职位不匹配。于是他们会试图内部调动或转岗，这最终又让公司陷入人才短缺的恶性循环。

（00:48:44）：所以我开始形成一套做法：在整个面试过程中，收集候选人未明言但暗示的担忧、恐惧和焦虑。到了录用阶段，我会发送一封不超过八个要点的邮件，直言不讳地指出可能加剧他们恐惧的现实。例如：“这里工作节奏快，周末也可能开会。” 又比如：“我是个家长，担心工作与生活平衡。” 这些担忧在面试中或许未被明说，但你能感知到其背后的真实需求。我作为家长也深有体会。

（00:49:31）：若是在初创公司，我会坦率说明：“我们是A轮融资的初创企业，正全力推动产品与市场的匹配。预期是10点准时到岗，偶尔周末加班。” 如果候选人能坦然接受这些条件，你就找到了A级人才；若他们犹豫不决，那与其让他们半年后离职，不如果断说：“对不起，这里不适合你。”

（00:50:08）：刚开始实施这套做法时，30%的候选人在录用阶段被淘汰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow.
turns.zh: 哇哦。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Which drove my recruiting partners insane because they look terrible. Their manager is like, "What the hell are you doing? You're losing everyone at the very end." And so they ask, "Can you either not send this thing?" Or, "Can you send it at the very beginning?" And my answer is no, because I don't know what they're afraid of yet. I have to go through the whole process to actually understand the thing that's going to potentially make them say no, and that's really crucial I think.
turns.zh: 这让我的招聘伙伴们抓狂了，因为那些邮件看起来糟糕透顶。他们的经理会说：“你到底在干什么？你最后把所有人都吓跑了！” 于是他们会问：“你能不能别发这封邮件？” 或者：“你能不能把它放在最前面发？” 我的回答是不能，因为我还不知道他们在害怕什么。我必须经历整个流程，才能真正理解可能导致他们拒绝的因素，而我认为这一点至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But once you hear it again, this is such an obviously good idea, clearly not an easy thing to do. In this case where recruiters were upset, is it just get buy-in from folks above, like, "Okay, this sucks for them, but at a macro level, this is good for the business" and they're like, "All right, let's keep doing it"?
turns.zh: 但当你重新审视这件事时，就会发现这显然是个好主意，但实施起来却绝非易事。在招聘人员感到不满的情况下，是否只需获得上级领导的认可，比如“好吧，这对他们来说确实不爽，但从宏观角度看，这对公司有利”，然后他们就会说“好吧，那我们继续吧”？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: At Square, at least, when I first started doing it, luckily I had a very good relationship with them. So that's a good starting point. This is maybe going to come across a little bit flippant, but they can't stop you from sending an email technically. So I'm just going to send the email. And if someone really wants to come and say, "This is bad for business," whatever it is, I have very strong reasons for why that's not the case. And now I've done it so many times, at least, that I can point to very clear proof points on why this is the right path.
turns.zh: 至少在Square公司，当我刚开始这么做的时候，幸运的是我和他们关系很好。所以这是一个很好的起点。说起来可能有点不敬，但从技术层面讲，他们无法阻止你发送邮件。所以我还是会发邮件。如果有人真想来反驳说“这对业务不利”之类的，我有充分的理由说明并非如此。如今我已经这么做了很多次，至少可以拿出非常明确的证据说明这条路是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In theory, the incentives would be aligned where the recruiter success matters. It's based on, did they actually have a good time? Did they stay? Did they have good impact?
turns.zh: 理论上，激励机制应该是与招聘成功挂钩的。关键在于，他们是否在公司度过了愉快的时光？是否留了下来？是否产生了积极影响？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But since they're not, obviously incentives aren't right.
turns.zh: 但显然，由于激励机制不当，他们并未做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I think some companies have shifted on that, where recruiters and salespeople are compensated sometimes in similar ways in terms of quota and whatnot. And so they'll hold the recruiter accountable to six, 12 post offer tenure before they say, "Oh yeah, you successfully landed this role." So you can tweak the incentive structure a little bit, but not everyone does that.
turns.zh: 我认为有些公司已经在这方面做出了调整，比如招聘人员和销售人员有时会以类似的方式获得销售配额等激励。这样一来，他们会让招聘人员对入职后的六个月、十二个月甚至更长时间负责，然后才会说“哦，对，你成功拿下了这个职位”。所以你可以稍微调整激励结构，但并非所有公司都会这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So the advice here is to end up with better people that end up being successful and happy. Keep track of the things that will probably be painful for them at the company, and then craft an email that shares upfront, "Here's what made be a problem if you join, and I just want to be very upfront about it." I think you actually shared a template of one of these emails in one of your blog posts.
turns.zh: 好的。所以这里的建议是最终招到更优秀、更成功且更快乐的员工。密切关注那些可能让他们在公司感到痛苦的事情，然后提前在邮件中坦诚说明：“如果加入我们，这里会遇到这些问题，我想提前把这些问题告诉你。”我记得你在博客文章中分享过其中一封邮件的模板。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Yep, that's right. I have a fairly real one in [inaudible 00:52:30].
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我在[00:52:30未录音]中有一个相当真实的例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else hiring-wise? I know there's probably infinite things that you've done, but is there anything else you think might be worth sharing of things you've learned to be more successful at hiring awesome people?
turns.zh: 招聘方面还有其他心得吗？我知道你可能有无数的经验，但你觉得还有什么值得分享的成功招聘秘诀吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: One final note I'll make on unsell email is it's not as if you just send the email and then they either say yes or no. Most of the time they will say, "Thank you. I am cool with six of these. This one freaks me out. Can we talk more?" Definitely. And I think this is where hiring managers have an incredible responsibility that sometimes isn't taken as seriously as it should, which is, when you are working with someone to get them to join or to offer, you need to bend to do whatever it takes for them. And so if they're like, "Hey, the only time I can talk is tonight at 11 o'clock after my kids go to bed." (00:53:18): "No problem. Here's my phone number, let's hop on. I will walk you through whatever you want to talk about." That sort of has to be the place you get to for really strong hires. So that's just one other thing I'll say. (00:53:29): The meta point around that is you need to be really invested in the candidates. This probably does change at a certain scale, like if you're "organization" is hiring a hundred engineers or whatever, you have process around it, you have pipelines, there's a machine at that point, but I do think the direct hiring managers have a responsibility to be really involved in every individual, because there's no one who's directly hiring a hundred people. It's always within a number that I think you can take on.
turns.zh: 关于未成功邮件沟通的最后一点说明：这并非你发送邮件后，对方要么同意要么拒绝那么简单。大多数情况下，他们会说：“谢谢。我对其中六个没意见，但这个让我有点担心。我们能再聊聊吗？”当然可以。我认为这正是招聘经理肩负的重大责任所在——但有时这份责任并未得到应有的重视。当你与候选人沟通，试图说服他们加入或接受录用时，就需要竭尽全力满足他们的需求。比如，如果对方说：“我唯一能沟通的时间是今晚11点，等孩子们睡下后。”你要回应：“没问题。这是我的电话号码，咱们现在就聊。想聊什么我都陪你。”这正是吸引优秀人才的关键所在。这只是我想强调的另一点。（00:53:29）关键在于，你需要全身心投入到候选人身上。这在大规模招聘中或许有所不同，比如当你的公司要招聘100名工程师时，可能会有标准流程和人才管道，但我认为直接招聘的经理有责任亲自参与每个候选的沟通，因为没有人能同时负责100人的招聘。这始终是可控的范围。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so this is the final tactic that I heard you're amazing at, which is automating user research. On the surface this sounds amazing. "I'm going to automate my user research. It's going to be amazing. So great." Talk about why you find this really powerful and important. And then how do you actually do this? How do you automate user research? How have you done this on your teams?
turns.zh: 好的，接下来是最后一个我听说你特别擅长的策略——自动化用户研究。表面上听起来很棒：“我要把用户研究自动化。这太棒了。太好了。” 能谈谈为什么你觉得这项技术如此强大和重要吗？然后具体怎么操作？如何实现用户研究的自动化？你在团队中是如何实践的？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Let's start from why this even matters. I think a lot of folks, going back to what is the point of product management, I think there's a similar overlap with UXR, like user experience research, and people will say, "Well, if they're doing research, what do I need to do? I should just be consuming what they're producing to help with that." (00:54:39): I know PM should settle for looking through bent glass in my opinion because whether it's a research report, whether it's something a salesperson is telling you, whether it's market research, don't care, it's been processed by someone, and PMs need direct exposure to raw material. End of story. And so that's where I think you just need to constantly be talking to or interacting with whoever is your customer. That's the foundation. (00:55:08): So okay, if we all agree on that, then the question is, "Well, I don't have time. It's so hard. How do I find them? My customer success manager says I can't talk to the client." If you are in a situation where the product manager is literally not allowed to talk to a customer, there is something structurally wrong and that needs to be fixed first. So I'm going to ignore that one for now just because that's a whole other rabbit hole, but you need to fix that in order to even get close to the next thing. (00:55:38): Okay, now the excuse is going to be, "Well, I don't have time. I don't want to run a program. I don't want to have to query and look up and send out emails every week." There's so many good resources out there right now, and I think that there are... I'll speak mainly from a B2B sense. I think B2C, slightly different story, I don't have as much experience there. But B2B, the two things I will say, one is, there's this thing called userinterviews.com. Shout out to them. They're pretty much user testing but explicitly focused on B2B and you can put in super clear criteria on the type of people you want to talk to. They do the heavy lifting and sourcing it, and then you just review and say, "Yes, yes. No, no," and you can have a steady stream of the exact ICP, you want to go after. ICP is ideal customer profile that you want to go after just coming to you automatically. Amazing. (00:56:28): The next one though, it depends on whether or not you have this tooling in place, but the broader theme behind this next category is your sales team is a research team, and if you don't view them that way, you are missing out on half the value. And so there's tools like Gong, which do call recordings, and you can set up filters and alerts for specific terms, phrases, competitors, whatever you want. I don't care what PM you are in the team. You can find the terms that are associated with what you care about the most. Those then get pushed automatically to a Slack channel or otherwise. And then you can set up workflows either via Zappy or something else to say, "Who was the customer? Pull their email, put that into a sequence, drop in my Calendly" and you just have interviews showing up automatically on your calendar. I will say I cannot take credit for this. Shout out to Beth Hills who was a PM that hired at Mutiny. She is the queen of automating customer research and built an amazing system around this.
turns.zh: 让我们先从为什么这很重要说起。我认为很多人，回到产品管理的核心意义所在，会发现它与用户体验研究（UXR）存在相似的重叠之处。人们会说：“既然他们在做研究，那我该做什么？我只需要消耗他们产出的成果就行了。” （00:54:39）：在我看来，产品经理不应满足于隔着扭曲的镜片看世界。无论是研究报告、销售人员的反馈，还是市场调研，都不重要——这些都经过了别人的过滤，而产品经理需要直接接触原始数据。就是这样。（00:55:08）：好吧，如果我们都认同这一点，那么问题来了，“我没时间。这太难了。怎么才能找到他们？我的客户成功经理说我不能和客户交流。” 如果你所在的公司根本不允许产品经理与客户沟通，那说明公司架构存在严重问题，必须先解决这个问题。暂且不讨论这个问题——那完全是另一个复杂的课题，但你必须先解决这个问题，才能谈下一步。（00:55:38）：好的，接下来会有人说：“我没时间。我不想运营一个项目。我不想每周都要查找、发送邮件。” 现在市面上有很多优质资源，我主要从B2B的角度来说。B2C的情况略有不同，我在这方面的经验不多。但对于B2B，我要提到两点：第一，userinterviews.com。向他们致敬。他们专注于B2B领域的用户测试，你可以设置非常明确的筛选条件，精准找到你想交流的目标人群。他们负责筛选和匹配，你只需筛选并确认即可。这样你就能源源不断地获得符合理想客户画像（ICP）的潜在客户，ICP就是你想要追逐的理想客户群体，信息会自动送到你面前。太棒了。（00:56:28）：接下来这部分取决于你是否有相关工具，但更深层的理念是，把销售团队视为研究团队。如果你不这么看待他们，那就错失了一半的价值。例如，Gong这样的工具可以录制通话，你可以设置过滤器和提醒，针对特定术语、短语、竞争对手等进行筛选。我不在乎你团队中的产品经理是哪位。你能找到与你最关心的内容相关的术语，然后这些信息会自动推送到Slack频道或其他平台。接着你可以通过Zappy等工具设置工作流，比如“客户是谁？获取他们的邮箱，添加到序列中，导入我的Calendly”，这样采访信息就能自动出现在你的日历中。我要强调，这不是我的功劳。向Beth Hills致敬，她是Mutiny公司招聘的产品经理。她是客户研究自动化的女王，围绕这个主题搭建了一个令人惊叹的系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the way it works is you set a term for like, I don't know, POS, point of sale, something in Gong, and if somebody says that or has an issue there, talk about again how that schedules a meeting with you potentially.
turns.zh: 具体操作是，你在Gong中设置一个术语，比如POS（销售点系统），如果有人提到这个术语或相关问题，系统会自动安排与你的会议。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Yes. So Gong has an integration with Slack. You set up this alert, it posts to Slack the excerpt of the transcript where it was mentioned along with the user or customer name. So in this case, it'll be Lenny's Burger shop. lenny@lennysburgershop.com, and then you can set up a Zapier to take every new Slack post from that and then send using, I don't know, customer.io in email to that person using that field. And then in that template of the email, drop in your Calendly specifically for user research.
turns.zh: 是的。Gong 确实与 Slack 集成了。你设置这个提醒后，Slack 会把提及用户或客户名称的对话摘录发布到群组中。在这个例子里，会是 Lenny's Burger 店，邮箱是 lenny@lennysburgershop.com。然后你可以用 Zapier 把 Slack 上的新消息抓取下来，再通过 customer.io 等工具发送邮件给相关人员。邮件模板里可以直接插入 Calendly 日程安排，专门用于用户研究。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is genius. I love that. There's another similar tactic that Teresa Torres shared on the podcast in one of the earlier episodes where you have a little popup on your homepage asking people, "Hey, do you want to talk? We'd love to hear feedback on our product. Click here if you want to give us some feedback," and then that schedules Calendly on the PMs.
turns.zh: 哇，这真是天才之举。我太喜欢了。特蕾莎·托雷斯在早期播客中也分享过类似策略：在主页上放个小弹窗，问用户“想聊聊吗？我们很想听听对产品的反馈。点击这里即可预约对话”，这样就能把 Calendly 日程安排到私信中了。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: PM's calendar. So you mentioned Gong, customer.io. There's some tools here. Zapier obviously. Is there anything else you find useful to help automate the sort of stuff?
turns.zh: 私信日历。之前你提到了 Gong、customer.io，还有一些工具，比如 Zapier。还有其他能自动化流程的工具吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: If I take a step back from the automation side or maybe straddle it, depending on the type of business you're in, there's ideally people talking about you somewhere, right? It's either happening on Reddit or Twitter or on some forum or your support forum. There is a community, there's a destination somewhere. And if there isn't, then I don't know, that's too bad. Maybe you don't have product-market fit. If you can take advantage of that, you can usually set up something. And if it's not a Gong or a Zapier, maybe it needs to be just a custom script that you write or you sit down with an engineer to say like, "How do we set up alerting around this thing so that I know when things are happening?" (00:59:36): I think you can't use the effort required to do that as an excuse to not be talking to your customers more frequently. Because again, if we go back to a product manager should be trying to convert this potential into kinetic energy, part of that understanding and part of knowing the constraints you can apply is just living in that world as much as possible. (00:59:59): The best comparison I can give is, there is a world of difference between reading a report about a lime cook and then standing with a lime cook. You will just pick up on so many ancillary aspects of what their life is like that cannot possibly be communicated in a report. You owe it to yourself as a PM to be exposed to those things all the time.
turns.zh: 如果不考虑自动化层面，或者说兼顾业务类型，理想情况下总会有人谈论你的产品吧？无论是在 Reddit、Twitter、论坛还是客服平台。总会有一个社区或交流平台。如果没有，那就太遗憾了。可能产品与市场不匹配。如果能利用这些信息，你通常能搭建起某种系统。即使不是 Gong 或 Zapier，也许只需要编写一个自定义脚本，或者和工程师一起探讨如何围绕这些信息设置提醒机制。（00:59:36）：我认为，不能以技术难度为借口，不去更频繁地与客户沟通。因为回到产品经理的角色，应该努力将潜在价值转化为现实动能。理解客户需求和应用约束的关键之一，就是尽可能多地沉浸在他们的世界中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In my experience, every time I talk to a customer, I'm always reminded, "Why have I not been doing this more? How can I not be doing this? It's absurd that I haven't done this," like every time you actually do it. But until you do that, you're like, "No, no, I know what they want. I'm reading all the customer service talent issues, I'm reading their emails, I get it." Until you actually talk to them, you're like, "Oh wow, I had no idea." (01:00:51): I love that your advice is like, the tactics you're sharing aren't, "Here's how you get a bunch of feedback." From your users, it's like, "Here's how you actually get to talk to the right users." It's like in the end of the funnel talking to a potential customer. It's not just reading a cool... some feedback that they shared.
turns.zh: 以我的经验，每次与客户交谈时，都会突然意识到：“为什么我之前没有更频繁地做这些事？为什么我不去做呢？真是太荒谬了。” 直到真正去做后，你才会感叹：“哇，我之前完全不知道。” （01:00:51）：我很欣赏你的建议不是那种“如何获取大量反馈”的套路，而是“如何真正与合适的用户对话”。这就像在漏斗末端与潜在客户沟通，而不只是阅读他们分享的反馈。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: That's right. I think just like the last point on this one is when you join a new team or start a new role, every PM is budding with energy to do this, "Of course I'm going to talk to my users." But then you reach a point where you go, "No, I know them inside and out. I don't need to talk to them anymore. I can write a PRD in my sleep. And I'm so busy doing both, product improvements, maintenance, annual planning, something else.I can use my intuition from the hundred interviews I've already done. I don't need to do one more interview." And that is a very tempting lie to tell yourself because the world is changing, their lives are changing, and you need to constantly be exposed to those little micro changes in their lives in order to build the product that they'll eventually need.
turns.zh: 没错。我觉得就像刚才提到的最后一点一样，当你加入新团队或开始新角色时，每个产品经理都充满干劲，迫不及待地想说：“当然要和用户交流啊！”但后来你会发现，自己已经对用户了如指掌，不需要再去沟通了。闭着眼睛都能写出PRD（产品需求文档）。但当你同时忙于产品改进、维护、年度规划等事务时，又会陷入另一个误区：用自己已经完成的上百次访谈积累的直觉经验，省去新用户调研的步骤。这是个极具诱惑的自我欺骗，因为世界在变，用户的生活也在变，你需要持续感知他们生活中的微小变化，才能打造出真正满足他们需求的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The best explanation I've heard of this is actually from your new boss, Patrick Collison, boss's boss's boss, I don't know how far away you're from him, where he talks about user research and where it fits in. And the way he described it is, instead of doing user research, talking to customers, informing what to build, it's talking to user, talking to customers informs your mental of what the customer needs and then that informs what to build.
turns.zh: 我听过的最好的解释来自你的新老板帕特里克·科利森——你应该离他不远吧——他在谈论用户研究及其定位时提到，用户研究不应只是收集信息、告知开发要做什么，而是要通过与用户对话，理解他们的真实需求，再以此为基础进行产品设计。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful way to think about it. (01:02:26): Okay, so I'm going to take us to a couple recurring themes of this podcast, a couple corners of this room that we have. First of all, I want to go to AI corner, so let's walk over there. Hello, AI corner. I'm curious if you've found any interesting uses of AI in your work or in your life.
turns.zh: 这个思路太棒了。（01:02:26）好的，我要带大家回顾本期播客的几个核心主题，以及我们讨论过的几个方面。首先，我们来聊聊AI专区。欢迎来到AI专区。想问问大家，在工作或生活中有没有发现AI的有趣应用案例？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: There's plenty in work. I don't know if any of them are interesting or novel. I feel like everyone's just figuring it out in real time together. So I'll actually take us in a slightly different direction. And this may be isn't directly useful to product managers, but I think it's a really good story. (01:03:02): So when Midjourney V1 was released, if we can remember that far back, it was at least I got beta access on a Saturday. And for what's worth, I have three daughters, one of them's seven years old, and so her and I were awake. We were waiting for the other two to wake up and I was like, "Oh, I have this cool new thing. Do you want to play with me?" And she goes, "Of course." So we log in, we create an account and I type in the first prompt, image gets generated, it's like a rainbow or something. And then I ask her, "Do you want to try it?" She goes, "Of course." So she types in unicorn prancing in a field and it generates this hideous looking demented unicorn with two rear ends and a demon flying over it. And I'm appalled at first thinking that she's going to feel really bad about what she got shown, but instead I look over and she's in awe. She is amazed. (01:04:04): And then she turns to me and she goes, "Did I draw that?" (01:04:06): "Yeah, I guess you did." And the thing that I got hung up on was that she used the word draw. She didn't say, "Oh, I enter a prompt and the LLM produced this thing," or whatever weird terminology that all of us use. It's like, "Did I draw that?" I don't know when it clicked for me, but at some point in time after that I was like, "The concept of these image generation models is the same as a crayon to her. There is no difference in her mind." And that is an insane change that I can't even comprehend. And so for me that's just been I think an experience that I go back to when I think about people asking, "What do you think AI is going to do and what's the next thing? And is it chat or is it something else?" I cannot comprehend what a child who grew up with a crayon of an LLM is going to think is a good product in 20 years. I need to start crying. But goddammit, I have no freaking clue. (01:05:11): And so I think I have a cheat code actually as a parent, because I get to see how they evolve and use these tools in real time. But all I can say is we are not even beneath the dust on the surface when it comes to what's going to change.
turns.zh: 工作中有很多事要做。我不知道有没有什么有趣或新奇的项目。感觉大家都在实时摸索中前进。所以我今天想带大家稍微转个方向。这虽然不一定对产品经理直接有用，但我觉得这是一个很棒的故事。（01:03:02）：当Midjourney V1发布时，如果大家还记得的话，我至少是在一个周六获得了测试资格。值得一提的是，我有三个女儿，其中一个七岁，那天早上她和我醒来后，等另外两个女儿醒来后，我问她：“哦，我有这个很酷的新玩意儿，你想和我一起玩吗？”她回答：“当然想。”于是我们登录、注册账户，我输入了第一个提示词，图片生成了一道彩虹之类的东西。然后我问她：“你想试试吗？”她说：“当然想。”她输入“独角兽在田野上跳跃”，结果生成了一只长着两个屁股、恶魔在头顶盘旋的恐怖独角兽。我一开始很震惊，觉得她会对看到的结果感到难过，但转头看时，她却惊叹不已。（01:04:04）：然后她转向我问：“这是我画的吗？” （01:04:06）：“对啊，我猜是你画的。” 让我印象深刻的是，她用了“画”这个词。她没有说：“哦，我输入了提示词，LLM生成了这个东西”，或者用我们常用的那些奇怪术语。她问：“这是我画的吗？” 我不知道什么时候突然意识到这一点，但在那之后的某个时刻，我突然意识到：“这些图像生成模型的概念，对她来说就像蜡笔一样。在她心目中没有区别。” 这是一个令人震惊的变化，我甚至无法理解。对我来说，当人们问：“你认为AI会做什么？下一步是什么？是聊天还是其他东西？” 时，这段经历就是我回想起来的例子。我无法想象一个在LLM陪伴下长大的孩子，20年后会认为什么是好的产品。我快要哭了。但天啊，我真的毫无头绪。（01:05:11）：所以我觉得作为家长，我其实有作弊码，因为我能实时看到他们如何使用这些工具。但我只能说，在即将发生的变革面前，我们连皮毛都还没触及。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is an amazing story, it gave me tingles. It makes me think a little bit about how we used to code in binary and then assembly and now it's Java, and then I don't know, all the languages, Python. And now it's like AI, LLM generating code and it's the same thing for drawing potentially. It used to be sticks on a cave and then became crayons and pens and iPads and all that stuff. And now it's again LLMs, so that's pretty bonkers. Amazing story. Thanks for sharing that. Useful to PMs and non PMs alike. (01:06:06): Okay, I'm going to take you to another recurring corner/segment of the podcast, fail corner. I'm curious if there's a story of failure that you can share of something that didn't go the way you wanted and still had a positive impact on your life or career?
turns.zh: 哇，这真是个令人惊叹的故事，让我起了一身鸡皮疙瘩。这让我不禁联想到我们过去如何用二进制编程，后来用汇编，现在用Java，还有Python之类的语言。现在又到了AI、LLM生成代码，可能对绘画也有同样影响。过去是洞穴里的石头，现在是蜡笔、钢笔、iPad之类的东西。现在又回到了LLM，这真是太疯狂了。很棒的故事。感谢分享。这对产品经理和非产品经理都很有用。（01:06:06）：好的，我要带大家进入播客的另一个固定环节——失败角。不知道大家有没有什么失败的故事，可以分享一下那些没有按预期发展，但对你的生活或职业产生积极影响的事情？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Well, there's countless stories of failure, but I'll choose the one that I think I've had to reference the most with people and has been to date the most difficult one to really talk about. I'm on the other end of it, and so now it's very easy, but it took several years to get there. (01:06:44): So context, I'm [inaudible 01:06:47] my way to PM, I land my first official, by title, PM job at a startup. I made it. I've arrived. I'm officially a product manager. And we go up, we go down, all the things happen. Fast-forward, the company is really struggling and so we go through a series of rolling layoffs and I'm round 4 something. At that point in time, my wife was nine months pregnant with our first child, and so I am freaking out. There is the personal side that I'm worried about, but then there's also my identity that has been completely crushed, because in the moment all I could think was, "I thought I was a product manager. This is evidence I am not," and I couldn't get past that. (01:07:37): And so for what it's worth, this is the one post I have on my website that I actually feel really, really proud of. It's called Finding Swagger. I can talk about why it's titled that way, but it's the thing that I really wrote more for myself because it's a good reminder to me every time I fall into this mentality again, because that may have been the first time that I really had the feelings of, "I'm not worth it" or, "I'm not meant to be this person," but it's recurred several times since then over the past decade. And when I read back through my mentality of how I got to the other end of it, it helps even myself sort of get back on the horse. (01:08:28): So okay, I get laid off, I'm distraught, I have no purpose, I'm nothing. And it was through a lot of reflection, a lot of conversation with friends and my wife where you eventually need to convince yourself that there is a difference between you not being good at something and a business or company not needing that thing at a particular moment in time, or you being very good at something but not in the way that a company needs. (01:09:01): And so I think once I was able to get to that, Square for me was the immediate subsequent role that I took on. And I went into that thing just full steam ahead, I'm going to prove myself. "I know I'm good," because I think I'm good, "and I am going to prove the hell out of that" mainly to myself, but ideally to other people too. (01:09:24): I think you shouldn't do things for other people for validation, but the initial success I got to see in launching a product, gaining the trust of my peers, having something that restaurants were texting me about, saying, "I can start my restaurant because of this. I didn't go down during rush hour because of this," that gave me the validation to say, "Okay, I am competent at this thing called product management." And then from there you can continue to build and continue to grow. (01:09:53): But I think right now, the market's weird, right? The market's wonky. There's a lot of really good talent that is just getting hit over sideways. I have a lot of friends that are having the same mental conversations around, "Well, I guess I'm just not worth it. I guess I wasn't cut out actually to do this job, do this role, be of this purpose." In some cases, maybe that's true and you can sort of have a career transition or a pivot in your life, but I think it's worthwhile to reflect on what are the things that were in your control that you can now change moving forward? And then what are the things that were truly out of your control that you can now apply to find a better fit? And that's one of the big things that I've been able to, I think, come around to. (01:10:41): And it's really hard because early on I think it's very tempting to associate a lot of different things with your identity. You're like, "I'm a startup guy. I'm a PM, I'm a fast whatever, I'm a fast thinker." And when an event happens that pokes at that part of your identity, the rest of it crumbles. And so long story short, I think it's really important for folks to use these moments where it feels bad and feels like a failure to reevaluate what parts are actually part of your identity and which parts are in your control to change in whatever you do next.
turns.zh:
嗯，失败的故事数不胜数，但我要讲的这个，我觉得是迄今为止我和别人提及最多、也最难启齿的经历。如今我已走出阴霾，但那段过程确实历经千辛万苦。（01:06:44）先讲背景吧，我一路晋升到产品经理职位，在一家初创公司获得了人生首份正式的产品经理头衔。当时我志得意满，觉得自己终于成功了。然而随之而来的是起起落落。快进到公司深陷困境，我们经历了一轮又一轮的裁员，我也成了第N批被裁的对象。当时妻子怀孕九个月，肚子里怀着我们的第一个孩子，我简直陷入了恐慌。一方面是为家庭担忧，另一方面是自我认同感彻底崩塌——当时我只想：“我以为自己是产品经理，但现在看来根本不是。” 这种自我否定的心态困扰了我很久。（01:07:37）所以说起来，这篇我网站上的文章《找到自信》，是我最引以为豪的作品。之所以取这个标题，是因为每次陷入自我怀疑时，这篇文章总能给我力量。大约十年前，那是我第一次产生“自己不配”、“不适合这份工作”的情绪，之后这种情绪又反复出现。回看当时的心路历程，能帮助自己重拾信心。（01:08:28）被裁后，我陷入迷茫，觉得自己一无是处。通过反思和与朋友、妻子的交流，我逐渐意识到，失败并不意味着自己能力不足，而是市场环境或公司需求的变化。（01:09:01）于是我转投Square公司，全力以赴证明自己。“我知道自己很优秀，”我对自己说，“而且我要用实际行动证明这一点”——这不仅是为了证明自己，也是为了让外界认可。（01:09:24）我认为不应为了他人的认可而行动，但当我成功推出产品、赢得同事信任、听到餐厅老板说“多亏了这个工具，我才能顺利经营”时，这种认可给了我信心：产品管理这件事，我确实能做好。自此，我得以持续成长。（01:09:53）但当下市场环境确实异常波动，很多优秀人才被迫转行。我身边许多朋友也在质疑自己：“看来我真的不行啊。”“或许我天生就不适合这份工作。”在某些情况下，转行或许是必要的，但更重要的是反思：哪些是我们可以改变的因素，哪些是超出我们控制范围的客观因素？
你们现在可以运用控制力来找到更适合自己的定位，对吧？这正是我逐渐领悟到的重要道理之一。（01:10:41）这真的很不容易，因为在早期阶段，我们总会把许多不同的身份标签与自己关联起来——比如“我是个创业者”、“我是个产品经理”、“我思维敏捷”等等。当某个事件触及你这些身份标签中的某个时，其他标签可能就会崩塌。长话短说，我认为人们必须利用那些令自己感觉糟糕、甚至认为自己失败的时刻，重新评估哪些部分才是真正属于你的身份标签，哪些部分是可以通过努力改变的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, what an important and great story. As you mentioned, a lot of people are dealing with finding it hard to find a new gig and a bunch of layoffs. I think this is going to help a lot of people. The two categories you shared I think are especially powerful. So the advice here is just separate, "This company just doesn't need someone with my skills right now" from, "I'm not good at these skills." Can you just share those two kind of things that might be true that you may not be recognizing about why they maybe laid you off again?
turns.zh: 哇，这真是个重要且意义非凡的故事。正如你所提到的，很多人都面临着找不到新工作和遭遇裁员的困境。我觉得这对很多人都会有帮助。你分享的两个分类观点尤其深刻。所以我的建议是，要把"这家公司现在不需要具备我这种技能的人"和"我不擅长这些技能"区分开来。你能否再分享一下可能导致被裁的两个真实原因，但自己却没有意识到呢？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally. So one is the business just doesn't have a need for you. They got ahead of their skis and that's their fault. They probably admit that, but that's not up to you. The second one though is my skills and the way that company operates are not compatible. This one I think is really, really important because I've seen so many times where there's been a PM engineer, designer, whatever role, they cannot make it work at company A, and then you see them five years later just killing it in company B and you're like, "Did they change as a person? Did they get super good at what they were bad at before?" Maybe a little bit, but honestly it was just a change in environment. And when you find the right environment in the right role, you just flourish. (01:12:40): And I think this is actually... Sorry, we'll go back to hiring for just a moment or at least management.
turns.zh: 没错。第一种情况是公司业务需求不足。这是他们的失误，他们可能会承认这一点，但这不取决于你。而第二种情况是你的技能与公司运营模式不兼容。这点我认为非常重要，因为我见过很多例子，比如某位PM工程师、设计师之类的角色在A公司做不好，五年后却在B公司大放异彩，你会觉得"他们变了吗"？可能有一点，但说实话更多是环境的不同。当你找到合适的环境和角色时，你就能大显身手。（01:12:40）：我觉得这实际上……抱歉，我们先回到招聘或至少管理层面的话题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 请继续。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: This is why performance conversations can always feel so difficult because it seems like you're telling someone you are bad, and as the recipient you're like, "I am bad." No one wants to hear that. But the reality is, you are not bad. It is that maybe the way that your environment is working, the machine that you exist as a part of, is not the kind that you thrive in. And so it's within your control to decide, "I'm going to change how I work to fit that environment" or, "I'm going to find a different environment that actually fits the way I work much better." And that's empowering.
turns.zh: 这就是绩效评估对话往往让人感到困难的原因，因为听起来像是在说你不行，而作为被评估者，你会觉得"我确实不行"。没人想听这种话。但现实是，你并非不行，而是你所处的环境、你所依附的那个"机器"，可能不适合你的成长。所以你可以选择改变自己去适应环境，或者寻找更适合你的新环境。这才是赋权。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that also applies a lot to interviewing. A lot of times you interview, don't get the job, and you exactly feel like, "Oh, I'm just not good enough." But really that company's way of working just may not gel with the way you operate. Like Uber operates very differently from Airbnb, operates very differently from Google. And so it's not that necessarily something you're doing wrong, they just don't think you're fit. (01:13:46): And this connects to something. I just had another guest on the podcast. He was a brain science dude, and he talks about how every company has this kind of habitat. What habitat are you creating for your employees to enable them to think differently or to be shut down and not feel like they can be creative or try big things or not? And basically, the way he just kind of to leverage that metaphor, like you may be a palm tree and you're trying to join Antarctica and it's not going to go well.
turns.zh: 我觉得这也适用于面试。很多时候面试失败后，你会觉得"哦，我就是不够好"。但其实可能是那家公司的运作方式与你的工作方式不匹配。比如Uber的运作方式与Airbnb、谷歌截然不同。所以这不一定是你的问题，而是他们觉得你不合适。（01:13:46）：这和另一个观点有关。我刚请来的一位嘉宾是脑科学专家，他谈到每个公司都有自己的"生态环境"。你为员工创造了怎样的生态环境，让他们能跳出固有思维、勇于尝试创新或挑战大项目？用他的话来说，你可能是一棵棕榈树，却想扎根南极洲，这肯定行不通。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You got to find Palm Springs or some hard place. Kevin, this has been amazing. Okay, so before we get to very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you think is important or valuable to share, leave listeners with? And if not, absolutely.
turns.zh: 你得找到棕榈泉或者其他艰难的环境。凯文，这次访谈太棒了。好的，在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你是否还有其他重要或有价值的观点想和听众分享？如果没有，那就结束了。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I think we'll probably find ourselves on interesting detours to the lightning round, so let's roll in.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们可能会在闪电问答环节走一些有趣的弯路，那就开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kevin, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 凯文，接下来我们要进入令人兴奋的闪电问答环节了。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Hell, yeah. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 当然啦，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. Question one, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，第一个问题：你向别人推荐过最多的两到三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I'll start by saying the type of book by volume that I read and get the most joy from are autobiographies and memoirs. It is just the ultimate cheat code to spend time with people that you respect, are interested by, or want to learn from. (01:15:05): Could you imagine what it would take in real life to sit down with Albert Einstein for 50 hours and just have him talk to you about his life? Impossible. But you can read and pretty much get the same thing. (01:15:21): So anyways, strong requirement or a strong suggestion, go read autobiographies and memoirs of people that you respect, mostly for their mental model and way to approach thinking, less about specific things. But the one book that I read without fail every year has a very misleading title. It's called The Courage to Be Disliked. I think it's been mentioned previously on the podcast, but it covers... It's a very Socratic method style, so it's about a philosopher and a young person, and it tries to teach you the ways of Adlerian psychology, which is sort of counter to Jungian theory. (01:15:56): The reason I really like it is because it makes me uncomfortable. So the whole premise, in my opinion, behind the book and other in psychology is focus on what you control. That's the one line. Don't worry about everything else. Don't worry about what other people think. Don't worry about what other people do. You cannot control those. You focus on yourself and you focus on the actions you can take. And be the person that you think will attract other people, that you want to be around. (01:16:29): There's some really pointed notes in there that I'm like, "Ha-ha-ha-ha. I don't fully agree with that one," but it always pushes me to question something about what I believe. And so in every physical copy of a book I have, I write the date that I started reading it again. The front inside cover of this book, I think it's been seven or eight years at this point that I've read it every single year.
turns.zh: 首先，我想说我最喜欢读的书类型是自传和回忆录。这简直是与你尊敬、感兴趣或想向其学习的人共度时光的终极秘籍。（01:15:05）：你能想象在现实生活中花50个小时和爱因斯坦坐下来听他谈论自己的人生会是怎样吗？不可能吧。但你可以通过阅读来获得类似的体验。（01:15:21）：所以，总之，我强烈建议或强烈推荐去读你尊敬的人的自传和回忆录，主要是为了获取他们的思维模式和思考方式，而不是具体内容。但每年我都会不间断读的一本书书名很误导人。它叫《被讨厌的勇气》。我记得之前在播客上提到过，但这本书采用苏格拉底式方法，讲述一位哲学家和一个年轻人之间的对话，试图传授阿德勒心理学，而这种心理学与荣格理论相悖。（01:15:56）：我特别喜欢这本书的原因是它让我感到不适。在我看来，整本书以及心理学的核心理念都是关注你能控制的东西。这就是核心。别担心其他事情。别在意别人的看法。别管别人怎么做。这些你都无法控制。你专注于自己，专注于你能采取的行动。成为你认为能吸引他人、自己也想与之共处的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. It's like a decision logging in another context almost.
turns.zh: 哇。这几乎像是在另一个语境下的决策记录。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Yeah, a little bit. I would say the other book I was going to mention is The Paper Menagerie. This actually shout out to Sean Rose for... I've never met him, but I really appreciate Sean. He was one of the early, if not, first PMs of Slack, and he used to be really loud on Twitter in a very good way, and I think I learned a ton from stuff that he would post. But one of the things that he posted was this book. It is just the most beautiful collection of essays that span sci-fi and fantasy. And so if you're into that kind of stuff, if you like exhalation, then Paper Menagerie is even better.
turns.zh: 是啊，有点像。我想提到的另一本书是《纸质动物园》。这里要特别感谢肖恩·罗斯……虽然我从未见过他，但我真的很欣赏他。他是Slack最早的PM之一，曾在Twitter上非常活跃，分享了很多有价值的内容，我从他发布的内容中学到了很多。但他分享过这本书。这是一本最美妙的散文集，涵盖科幻和奇幻题材。所以如果你喜欢这类作品，如果你喜欢《呼气》，那么《纸质动物园》就更棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, shit. Guess I got to add this book to my list. I do love exhalation.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。我得把这本书加到我的书单里了。我确实喜欢《呼气》。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 好的，就这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man, this job is tough. I get to learn all these amazing books and then I got to read them, but I don't have time. Hard. (01:17:51): Speaking of more time, next question. Do you have any favorite recent movies or TV shows that you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 天哪，这份工作真是太难了。我得学习所有这些精彩的书籍，然后还要去读它们，可我根本没时间。太难了。（01:17:51）：说到更多时间，下一个问题。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: There's less time for either these days. I will say not novel, the Bear holds a very special place in my heart right now, both because I worked in restaurants and I got to build for them. And so seeing the details that they do actually gives me a lot of anxiety, but I really appreciate the craft they put into it. (01:18:16): The other show, actually, I think this is the first time, Physical 100. So this is a Netflix show. It's a Korean show about a hundred different bodybuilders, athletes, what have you, on who has the optimum physique or whatever. I don't really care about that part. The two things I love about the show are, one, it's ridiculous what people are capable of. You see what they can physically do and you're like, "Oh my God, that's amazing what they can put their minds to." The other part though, and this is maybe a trend of Korean shows that I've noticed, is the amount of respect they have in this competition is bar none. You have this guy who is historically famous, was the top champion in judo or something, and you have all these other athletes that are 15, 20 years younger, and they're bowing and just humble to compete against the guy. I kind of wish that more American Joes had that level of respect as opposed to just trying to find the most conflict. There's something that I really like about that.
turns.zh: 最近没时间做这些了。我要说不是小说，《熊的故事》现在在我心里占据着一个特殊的位置，一方面是因为我在餐厅工作过，能为他们建造东西。看到他们做的那些细节真的让我很焦虑，但我真的很欣赏他们投入的精工技艺。（01:18:16）：另外一部剧，实际上这是我第一次提到，《Physical 100》。这是Netflix的韩国剧，讲一百个不同的健美运动员、运动员之类的，比拼谁拥有最佳体型之类的。我对这部分没兴趣。我喜欢这部剧的两点，一是人们能做到的太不可思议了。你看到他们的身体极限，简直惊叹于人类意志的力量。另一点，我注意到韩国剧有个趋势，就是比赛中的人们对彼此的尊重达到了极致。比如有个历史上有名的柔道冠军，年龄比参赛选手大15、20岁，选手们都鞠躬致敬，表现得非常谦逊。我真希望美国人能多些这种尊重，而不是总想制造冲突。这点我很欣赏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's beautiful. I've started that show, but I haven't continued it, so I'm going to revisit it.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我开始看这部剧了，但没继续下去，我要重新看一遍。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product that you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: We got a really old 2002 Jeep to work on with my daughters, just like a true junker. And as a result of that, we're repairing it. We're taking off the rust, replacing parts, and so there's these little magnetic trays that you can hold screws and nails and whatnot, so they don't go flying and rolling around everywhere. It's stupidly useful when you're working on a car. And the girls love it because they can use it for other things like collecting hair clips or whatever else. So magnetic trays, shout out. (01:20:06): And then selfishly, I will say my buddy Arjun Mahanti has an app called Circuit. If you search the app store for Circuit, like C-I-R-C-U-I-T, HIIT timer, it's such a delightful little app that lets you track Tabata sex or whatever else to just get a little workout in.
turns.zh: 我们有一辆2002年的老旧吉普车要修理，和女儿们一起弄的，就是一辆真正的破车。结果我们一直在修理它，除锈、更换零件，还有那些能吸附螺丝、钉子之类的小磁吸托盘，这样东西就不会到处乱飞。在修车时真是太实用了。女儿们也很喜欢，因为她们还能用它来收集发夹之类的东西。所以磁吸托盘值得推荐。（01:20:06）：另外说点自私的，我朋友Arjun Mahanti有个叫Circuit的应用。如果你在应用商店搜索Circuit，首字母大写，HIIT计时器，这款应用太棒了，能记录塔巴塔训练之类的，随时锻炼一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super cool. Magnetic tray is not boring at all. That is extremely cool and it has a really cool story too. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to and find useful to share with friends and family in work or in life?
turns.zh: 太酷了。磁吸托盘一点也不无聊。太酷了，背后还有个很棒的故事。你有没有特别喜欢的座右铭，经常回味，觉得很有用，可以分享给工作和生活中的朋友家人？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I think we've actually maybe touched on both of these. I'll cheat and I'll pull one from maybe each parent so that in case they see this, they don't feel like I'm favoring one of them. (01:20:45): So my mom's side, I think something that she would always repeat to me growing up is everything happens for a reason. I hated that growing up because she only said it when something bad would happen. Something bad happens, she goes, "Everything happens for a reason," and I'm like, "No, it doesn't. Life just sucks." And to no surprise at this point in the conversation, I've now grown to really, really appreciate that piece of advice because what it's actually trying to communicate is, when something happens, good or bad, frankly, don't dwell on it. That's the past. Focus on what you want to do and then just move towards that. And then in most cases, you'll be able to look back in one, five, 10 years and connect the dots in a way where the story makes sense in your mind. And so just having that shift in perspective I think has helped me a lot to not overreact to anything that happens in my life. So that's one side. (01:21:46): And then on my dad's side, so the funny origins of this, unsurprising to anyone with Asian parents, I'm a spunky little 7-year-old, I come home with my math test one day. I got 97%. I think that's pretty good. I go show it to my dad with beaming eyes and pride. He sort of stares down his nose at it, looks at me, "Where's my other 3%?"
turns.zh: 我觉得我们可能已经提到了这两点。我就偷个懒，每边各举一个例子吧，这样万一父母看到这段内容，他们就不会觉得我偏向其中一方了。（01:20:45）：说到我母亲那边，我记得她在我成长过程中经常对我说的一句话是"凡事皆有因"。小时候我特别讨厌这句话，因为她总是在坏事发生后才说这句话。比如出什么问题了，她就会说："凡事皆有因。"我当时就会说："才怪！生活就是这么糟糕。"不出所料，随着时间推移，我现在越来越欣赏这条建议了。因为它的核心意思是，当好事或坏事发生时，别纠结于过去。过去的已经过去，专注于你想做的事，然后朝着目标前进。大多数情况下，五年、十年后，你回头看时，会发现事情的脉络逐渐清晰。所以这种思维转变真的帮助我避免对生活中的突发状况反应过度。接下来是父亲那边。说起这段趣事，对有亚洲父母的人来说并不意外。我当时还是个活泼的7岁小女孩，有天带回家数学考试卷，得了97分。我觉得还不错，就兴高采烈地拿给父亲看。他却冷淡地看着卷子，问："另外3%在哪儿？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, my God.
turns.zh: 天哪！

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: I'm just distraught and I sulk away. I'm very sad. I study hard. I do the next math test, I get 100% yes. All right, dad's approval, here we come. I come flying back, I put the test in his hands, he stares down his nose at it, looks at me, "Where's my other 3%?" I'm so confused. I'm like, "I got 100 out of 100. I have no clue what you're talking about." He just looks me down the eye and goes, "Who said a hundred is the most you can get?" At that age, I literally had no clue what he was talking about. And he had to reframe it for me in the moment around like, "Well, was there extra credit? Can you just write your own problems to challenge yourself more? Could you have given yourself another test? And maybe the teacher won't give you credit, but you give yourself credit for doing additional work." (01:23:01): I think I carry that theme forward where there's this weird transition we all go through from childhood to adulthood where we no longer receive homework, we're responsible for defining the work that we do. And when you do that, if all you do is the minimum of what defined the 100% of what your job requires, you'll never grow. And so it's up to you to actually find what is the additional 3%? There's always three more percent. So that's my dad's lesson.
turns.zh:
我气坏了，闷闷不乐地走开了。我很伤心，一直努力学习。下次考试我考了100分，终于得到父亲的认可了。我兴高采烈地跑回去，把卷子递给他，他还是冷冷地问："另外3%在哪儿？"我完全懵了。我说："我考了100分啊，不知道你在说什么。"他只是一脸不屑地说："谁说100分就是最高分了？"
在那个年纪，我真的不明白他的意思。他当场给我重新解释："那有没有额外加分项？你能不能自己出题挑战自己？再多做几套卷子？老师可能不给你加分，但你自己给自己加分。"
（01:23:01）：我觉得这段经历也延续到了我从童年到成年的成长过程中，那段奇特的过渡期——我们不再接受作业，开始自主规划工作内容。如果你只做最低限度的工作，就永远无法成长。所以关键在于去探索那额外的3%空间。总会有3%的提升空间的。这就是我父亲给我的启示。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kevin, you're blowing my mind. There's so many great stories, you're just full of them. And I feel like this lesson also applies really well to product and building product and founding companies.
turns.zh: 凯文，你真是让我惊叹不已。你有太多精彩的故事了。我觉得这条经验教训也非常适用于产品开发、创业公司创立等领域。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just pushing further than people expect and making it a lot more delightful than the minimum bar. (01:23:53): Final question, speaking of things that maybe people don't expect and may not understand is possible, looking at you, nobody would've guessed that you're a competitive eater at some point in your life. As a final question, tell us about this part of your life. What did you eat? How does this work? How far did you get in this path?
turns.zh: 只需超越人们的预期，让事情比最低标准更有趣。（01:23:53）：最后一个问题，说到人们可能不期望或不理解的事情。看看你，任何人都不可能猜到你曾在人生某个阶段是一名竞技吃货。作为最后一个问题，请和我们分享这段经历。你都吃了些什么？这条路走得有多远？

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: It's probably misleading to say that I was a true competitive eater. I wasn't on the circuit with a... I forget his name, but Johnny Chestnut.
turns.zh: 说自己是真正的竞技吃货可能有些误导。我从未加入过巡回赛……我忘了他的名字，但约翰尼·切斯特纳特（Johnny Chestnut）确实是这个领域的先驱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 01:24:21]. Oh yeah, Chestnut
turns.zh: [01:24:21的背景音]。哦，对，切斯特纳特。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: Back in the day, that's like the OG competitive eater on the hotdog circuit, I guess.
turns.zh: 在过去，他可是热狗赛事界的元老级人物吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: For me it was more eating challenges. And so whenever I would travel, I would find the local eating challenge, whether it was time-based, volume-based, something else, and just try to see what I could push my body to do. I was blessed with a great metabolism, so I never really had to worry too much about anything else. And the origin, the first moment of this was when I was 14, my sister was going to college in Minnesota and there's this steakhouse up there called Manny's, which is where the Vikings Frontline goes to after every game. And they have this ridiculous 97 ounce order house. I don't know how many pounds that is, but it's too much meat for a human to consume.
turns.zh: 对我来说，更多的是参加各种吃播挑战。每次旅行时，我都会寻找当地的挑战赛，无论是限时挑战、量化挑战还是其他形式的，看看自己能把身体推向何种极限。我天生新陈代谢旺盛，所以从不必过多担心。这一切的起点是14岁那年，当时我姐姐去明尼苏达州上大学，那里有一家叫Manny's的牛排馆，维京人队的后防线队员赛后常去那里。他们有份离谱的97 盎司牛排套餐。我不知道具体换算成磅数，但那量肉对普通人来说实在太过分了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 97 ounce.
turns.zh: 97 盎司。

turns.speaker: Kevin Yien
turns.en: 97 ounces, yeah. And so I sit down, I order it thinking, "This is going to be great." They put it in front of me, it's a monster. You have to eat in under an hour. And so 45 minutes into it, I'm halfway through and about to die. And the catch is, if you finish it in under an hour, you get it for free. And so my dad again leans in and goes, "You can't afford not to finish this." (01:25:39): And so, "Message received, sir." Hunker down. I plowed the other half in 15 minutes. I then slept for I think three days afterwards. But after that I was like, "Oh my God, if I could do that, what else could I do?" And so, [inaudible 01:25:54] carried for, I don't know, nearly a decade of trying to do these interesting challenges.
turns.zh: 97 盎司，对。于是我点了餐，心想：“这肯定很棒。”他们把餐端上来时，那堆肉简直是个巨无霸。必须在一小时内吃完。45分钟后，我已经吃了一半，快累死了。关键是，如果能在一小时内完成，就可以免费获得这份餐。于是我爸爸又凑过来说，“你必须完成，否则后果自负。”（01:25:39）：“明白了，先生。”于是我埋头苦干，15分钟内吃完了剩下的部分。之后我睡了整整三天。但从那以后，我就在心里想：“天啊，如果我能做到这些，还有什么事是我做不到的呢？” 于是，[01:25:54的背景音]，我花了将近十年的时间尝试各种有趣的挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I don't know how that's physically possible, but clearly you did it. (01:26:02): Kevin, this has been wonderful.
